OLD  AND  NEW  STYLE
The Julian  Year,    introduced  by Julius  Caesar,    45 years  B.  C.,
made every fourth year,   without exception,   a leap year.            This  was
anover-correction, -an error of seven days in 900 years.         As early
as the year 1414 it was perceived that the equinoxes were gradually
moving from the 21st of March and September,    where they ought
aways to have fallen had the Julian year been exact.       A new reform
ofthe calendar was thus required;   and it took place under the pope-
domof Gregory XIII,  by the omission of ten nominal days after the
4th of October,   1582,   so that the next day was called the 15th,    and
not the 5th.          This change was immediately adopted by all  Roman
Catholiccountries, but tardily in the countries of Protestantism.
In England the change of style,  as it was called,   took place after
the  2d day of  September,    1752,     eleven  nominal  days being  then
struck out,     so that the last day of the Old Style being the 2d,    the
first  of the New Style (the next day) was called the 14th instead of
the  3d.         The  same  legislative   enactment   which  established   the
Gregorian year  in England  in 1752  shortened  the  preceding  year,
1751,   by a full  quarter.       Previous to that time the year was held
to begin with the 25th of March,   and the year 1751 accordingly did
so,   but that year was not suffered to run out,  being supplanted on
the 1st of January by the year 1752,   which,   it  was enacted,    should
commence on that  day;   therefore during  the  months of January,
February and March of that year double datings were used,    thus,
February  22,      1751-52,    one being  the Old Style  and the other  the
New Style.

GENEALOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES
ABBOTT
HIRAM  EMERY  ABBOTT ( Thomas,        Enos,        Jonathan,        John,
John,       Thomas¹) was born at Rumford,  Me. ,  23 Jan. 1827 ;   married at
Braintree,     Harriet Newell Johnson.      She died 15 Nov.  1854,   age 24
years,    and was buried in the Village Cemetery at the Landing.        (De-
scendants  of  George,    Daniel,      Thomas  and  Robert  Abbott,     1906,
p.     947.)
ABELL (ABLE)
•  ROBERT ABELL desired to be made a freeman of the  Massachu-
setts Bay Colony,   19 Oct.  1630,  and took the freeman's oath 18 May,
1631.    He early had six acres granted to him "in the plaine. "    (Wey-
mouth LandGrants,  262,  267,  273.)     His wife was Joanna  -, who
survived him.         The family removed to Rehoboth in 1643.   He prob-
ably came in the fleet with Governor Winthrop.       The settlement  of
his  estate,       9 Aug.  1663,    mentions  "his  eldest  son,  his  widow,    his
daughter Mary and his five children."    (Register,   6:   96.)
Children,born at Weymouth:
Abraham,    bur.  14 Nov. 1639.
Mary,  b.   11 Apr. 1642.
ADAMS
JOHN ADAMS of  Braintree,    afterwards second  President  of  the
United States,   married at  Weymouth,   25 Oct.  1764,   Abigail Smith,
daughter ofRev. William and Elizabeth Smith of the North Parish of
Weymouth.             They resided in that part of Braintree  (now Quincy)
near the Quincy Adams station on the New York,  New Haven and
Hartford Railroad,   and the house in which they lived is still  (1920)
standing.           (See the Genealogical History of Henry Adams,    1898.)
NATHANIEL¹  ADAMS,   a  dish-turner,   had land granted to him
between  1642  and  1644.    Four  of his  five  lots were in the  "East
field. "    He was  born  near  1601,     and  his  wife's  name was  Sarah.
He was made a freeman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony,   26 May,
1647.    Heremoved to Boston before 1652.    Hemust be distinguished
from  Nathaniel  Adams  of  Boston,    who by a wife,    Mary,    had ten
children born  in  Boston,     1653 to  1677.    Nathaniel Adams,   Sr.,      of
Boston,   dish-turner,  "being aged," made his will 14 July,   1675,    be-
queathing to his wife Sarah,   sons Nathaniel,  David,  Abraham,   Jona-
thanand to IsaacAdams if he be alive and shall return to Boston,   to
grandchild  Sarah,   daughter  of  son  David Adams,    and grandchild
David,   son of David Adams.      To Mary Timewell £10 as a token of

RICHARD¹  ADAMS (a servant to William Read who came from
Batcombe,   county of Somerset),  aged  "29 yeare, "  Mary,   his wife,
aged "26 yeare"  and Mary "Cheame," his daughter,   aged 1 "yeare, "
sailed  from  Weymouth in Dorsetshire  in  Rev. Joseph Hull's Com-
pany on or about 20 Mar. 1634-35,   and arrived at Dorchester 7 June,
1635.    He was  made a freeman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony,
2 Sept. 1635,    and had seven lots granted to him in Weymouthbetween
1635  and 1644.    He probably came from Dorsetshire  or  Somerset-
shire,   and may have sailed as a servant to disguise his identity.       He
waselected from Weymouth a Deputy to the Great andGeneral Court
which was held at Newtowne (Cambridge),   2 Nov.  1637,      and again
12 Mar.  1637-38.           He,    or his family,   was somehow related  to John
Bibbell  (Bibble)  of Boston and Malden,    who made his  will at Hull,
21  July,    1653,    by which Adams,     his  wife and five children each re-
ceived twelve pence apiece.        (Register,    9:    307.)     He was a planter
and removed to Malden before 10 Apr. 1649.    Further details of this
family are to be found in The Descendants of Thomas Wellman of
Lynn,    1918,    pp.   84-86.
Children,  born at Weymouth,   except the first :
Mary Cheame, 2  b.    in England near 1633.
Sarah,   b.    3 July,    1637.
Samuel,    b.    6 June,    1639.
Ruth,   b.    3 June,   1642.
WILLIAM ADAMS,  by his wife Susanna,  had born at Weymouth,
a son,
William,   b.    26 Aug. 1686.

AGER
This surname is found inAgar, Agard, Aggar, Agur, Eager,   Eagers,
Eagr,    Eagure,    and similar forms.        No distinguishing  characteristics
are to be found in the name itself.
1.    RICHARD  AGER,  a shipwright,   resided  in Weymouth,    from
1698 to  1719.     He married Abigail Nash,   daughter of Lieut.     Jacob
and Abigail (Dyer) Nash,  born at Weymouth,  17 Aug. 1673.
Administration on his estate was granted to his son,   Richard Ager
of Weymouth,   cordwainer,  11 Jan.  1724-25.          (Suffolk  Probate Rec-
ords,    23:    463.)    He died at  Weymouth,   8 Nov.  1719.    In his will,
dated 4Jan. 1716-17,   Jacob Nash of Weymouth gave 50 acres of land
to his "daughter Abigail Eager. "     (Ibid.    20:   391.)
Children, born at Weymouth:

Braintree.

ALGER
JOHN  ALGER,   son  of  Andrew Alger  of  Scarborough,      Me.  ,      of
Boston,    made his  will with a power of attorney,   4 Apr.  1690.    He
calls  himself John Alger,   carpenter,    formerly of Weymouth,    residing
in Charlestown,   and grants power of attorney to his only sister Eliza-
beth to receive his wages and effects.       Witnesses :    Samuel Phipps and
Hannah Adams;   recorded 11 June,  1716.    (Suffolk Probate. )

ALLEN                                     11
THOMAS ALGER came in the Charity or Swan,  arriving at Wes-
sagussett  in June or July,   1622,   in Weston's Company from Newton
Ferrers  in Devonshire.          He was one of the four who escaped death,
and was now (1624) at Christopher Levett's plantation at Casco on the
coast of Maine.          (Levett's Voyage,   1623-24,   published in Collections
of the Massachusetts  Historical Society,    Third Series,   8:     158-190.)
Inaletter which John Winter wrote to Robert Trelawny,  7 Oct.  1640,
Winter says that certain men "did know the  River of Casco before
your  pattent  was  granted, "   and  among  them  names :          "Thomas
Alger of Newton Ferrers,   which dwelt at the house at Casko about 10
yeares  since. "     (Trelawny Papers,   250-251.)    That house was prob-
ably built  by Christopher  Levett  in  1624,   and Alger was one of the
inhabitants of it  in 1630.    Another letter from Winter to Trelawny,
datedatRichmond's Island, 7 Oct. 1640,  states that Thomas Alger was
employedby Trelawny "the first yeare" on his plantation from 2 Mar.
1633,    to 18 June,   1634.    (Ibid.    244.)     Winter did not know if he were
living in 1640.    He may,   or may not,  be the Thomas Alger who ap-
pears at Taunton in 1665.

deceased.             His  widow Anna resided  in South Weymouth in  1896.
(Norfolk Probate,  31860.)    His wife was a native of Landgrove,  Vt.

ALLISON
WALTER  HARRIS  ALLISON,   son  of  William  Davidson  and
Amey (Adlington) Allison,   was born in Boston,   31 Oct. 1814;   died 9
Sept.  1857,    age 42 years 10 months 9 days.        He enteredhis intention
of marriage at Weymouth,  23 Jan. 1836 (married 9 Feb. 1836)  with
Mary Whitmarsh.         She  was born 4 Oct.  1813,   and died at Wey-
mouth,      1  Mar.  1903;  both buried in the Village  Cemetery at  the
Landing.           He was a tailor and resided in Boston,  Braintree,   Lexing-

14                             APPLEGATE-ARNOLD
APPLEGATE
THOMAS APPLEGATE,   a planter,  "was licenced to Keepe a ferry
betwixte  Wessaguscus  & Mount Woolliston for wch hee is to have
1dfor evy pson and iii d a horse," by the General Court holden " att
Newe Towne"   (Cambridge),     2 Sept.  1635.      (Massachusetts  Bay
Colony Records,    1:    156.)    The General  Court  discharged him "of
Keepeing the ferry of Waymothe, " 3 Mar. 1635-36.          (Ibid.    165.)    His
wife,   Elisabeth   -, was censuredby the Court, 6Sept. 1636.   (Ibid.
177.)    He lost a canoe in a drowning accident before 4 Dec. 1638,   and
the General Court allowed him 29 shillings for his canoe,    "when the
armes wch hee borrowed are returned,"  5 Mar. 1638-39.         ( Ibid.      246,
248.)
The land first granted to him "on the plaine" was later granted to
JohnAllin,   and the town voted to grant him lots "on the East side of
Great Pond" before 2 Feb. 1651-52.         (Weymouth Land Grants,    255,
281.)     He had a suit in Plymouth Colony Court on or about 1 June,
1641.    (Plymouth Colony Records,   2:18.)    He settled in Weymouth
prior to thecoming of the Hull Company and was an inhabitant there
from  1635 to 1651,   at least.      He was associated at Weymouth with
Thomas  Rawlins,    John King,    George Allen  and William  Newland
about  1638.    (Lechford's   Note-Book,     392.)    A John  Applegate,
whose mother was Elizabeth, was living at Oyster Bay,   L. I. ,   in 1685.

28 Mar. 1676.     (Nash's History,   39.)

•    THOMAS¹  BAILEY resided in Gloucester from 1699 to 1704.   He
died at Gloucester,    15  Oct.  1704.    His wife was named Mary
and three  children were born at Gloucester,    or Cape Ann.           Two of
those  children were recorded on Weymouth Town Records as born
"att  Cape-Pan. "     It  is  fair  to  assume that those children removed
from Gloucester to Weymouth,   and that their names and births were
recorded at Weymouthafter their father's death.
. Children,  bornat Gloucester,  recorded at Weymouth:
Thomas, 2  b.     27 Feb. 1699-1700.
Samuel,    b.     16 Aug. 1702;  not recorded at Weymouth.
Mary,    b.     26 or 27 Oct.  1704.

BAKER
EDMUND BAKER came in the Charity or Swan to Wessagussett
in June or July,   1622,   in Weston's  Company.     He was one of the
"four menwhich escaped" to Christopher Levett's plantation in 1623
and related to him the condition of Weston's Colony.       He came from
Newton Ferrers in Devonshire and "dwelt at the house at Casko with
 - 26 - 
22                         BARKER -BARTLETT -BATES
ThomasAlger about 10yeares past" (1630).           (Trelawny Papers,   251.)
He was one of the men "that did know the River of Casco before
[Trelawny's]     pattent  was  granted. "    (Ibid.        250.)      Winter  did not
know whether he was living 7 Oct. 1640.
BARKER
JOSEPH  BARKER and his wife Ruth        were called,    in the will
of Dorothy (Hunt)   King of  Weymouth,    made 14 June,   1652,       "my
son" and "my daughter, "  the former being made executor of said will.
The testator was the wife of John King,  seaman,   of Weymouth,    and
formerly the wife of Enoch Hunt of Weymouth,    1639 to 1647.   The
testator  had a daughter,    Sarah  Hunt,     born at Weymouth,    4 July,
1640,   unmarried on 14June,    1652,   and another daughter called Susan-
nah  Heath  on the last-named date.            It  is  evident  that  Susannah
Heath was,     on 14 July,    1652,     the wife  of Peleg Heath of Roxbury.
Children of Peleg and Susannah Heath,    born and baptized at Rox-
bury,     were  Susannah,    bp.     5  Dec.  1652;     Hannah,    b.    23  Dec.  1654;
Abigail,    b.     10 Oct. 1658;   Joseph,  b.  23andbp.   30 Dec. 1660,   d.    in a few
days;   Mehitable,  b.  7 Feb. andbp.  9 Mar. 1662;   William,   b.   30 Jan. ,
andbp.   6Mar. 1664;  Joseph,   2d,  b.   6,   and bp.   16 Sept. 1666,    d.   1674;
Peleg,   b.    18 Sept.,   and bp.     22 Nov.  1668;   Dorothy,    b.   18 Dec. 1670.
Peleg,     the father,  was buried 18 Nov. 1671.    He was the son of Wil-
liam Heath,     and came from London with his father's family  in the
Lion,    arriving  16 Sept.  1632.
Was Dorothy (Hunt-King) the mother of Joseph Barker or of Ruth,
his wife?
Dorothy Barker was admitted to the First  Church of Dorchester
before 4 Nov.  1639.    (See  Register,  5:  239. )    She was probably the
mother ofJoseph Barker,  and three times a widow.
BARTLETT

Braintree and Mendon.          He removed to Mendon.
Child,  born at Weymouth:
John,   b.    11 Feb.  1666.

44.  JOSHUA BATES  (Joshua,       Abraham,      John,     Edward,      Ed-
ward¹),   son of Joshua and Tirzah,   born 10 Oct.  1788;  died  24 Sept.
1864,     aged 75 years  11  months  16 days;    married Lucretia Augusta
Sturgis,    daughter of  William and       ;  she died 22 June,   1863.
Children:
William  Rufus Gray,  b.    11 July,   1815,   killed while hunting,    22
Dec. 1834.
,  a daughter,    who married M. Sylvain Van der Weyer,  Belgian
Minister to St. James.
He was born in Weymouth,  midway between the North and East
Villages.       He was educated in the public schools,    and under the tuition
of Rev. Jacob Norton,   but on account of weak eyes did not enter a
college course.
In 1803 he entered the counting room of William Rufus Gray,   and
there  laid  the foundation of his  mercantile  career.           About 1813 he
formed a partnership with Captain Beckford of Charleston,   but it  was
dissolved in three years .
In 1816 he was sent  to  England as the confidential agent of Hon.
William Gray,    and so gained the confidence of the mercantile public,
that Mr. Caesar Labouchere of Amsterdam (a connection of the Bar-
ings)   loaned  him $100,000  to  enter  the  banking  business  with  Mr.
John Baring,   and in two years they were both admitted to partnership
in the great banking house of Baring Bros. & Co. of London,  of world-
widefame.
This firm was the fiscal agent and banker of the United States,    and
hisposition enabled him to be of the utmost service to his native coun-
try in the troublous times that followed.
He was  umpire,    with  two  commissioners,     to  settle  unadjusted
claims that resulted from the War of 1812;  and this,   with his many
other services,  showed the estimation in which he was held by the gov-
ernments of both countries.
It is related that he was offered the title of knighthood,   but he pre-
ferred"to remain a simple American citizen. "
Remembering his  early  days  in  Boston,   he gave in 1852 $50,000
as a fund for  the purchase of books for  the Boston Public Library,
and also  presented it  with about 47,000 volumes,     thus becoming the
founder of one of the greatest educational institutions that we possess.
Bates Hall in that institution was named in his honor.
He lies buried,   with his wife and son,  in the Kensal Green Cemetery
at London,    Eng.

70.    BRIG.          GEN.           JAMES   LAWRENCE   BATES    ( Elijah,
Samuel,            Jonathan,        John,        Increase,         Edward¹) ,    son of  Elijah  and
Sally,     was born 6 Aug. 1820;    died 11  Nov. 1875;      married Betsey D.
Loud,    16 Apr. 1851,   daughter of Quincy and Hannah W. Loud,  born
30 Dec. 1829;     she died 14 Sept. 1853,  aged 24 years 8 months 15days.
 - 49 - 
BATES                                       45
Child:
-, daughter,  b.  20Sept. 1852;  d.   21 Sept. 1852,  ae.  1 d.
He married for  second wife widow Mary J. Hersey,  24 Jan.  1856,
daughter of James and Betsey (Whitmarsh) Tirrell,  b.   1826.
Children:
James Wilmot,  b.   20 Nov. 1856;   d.    11 Aug. 1887.
Annie Tirrell,    b.  30 May,   1858;   d.   25 Feb.  1880.
Betsey Tirrell,  b.   16 July,  1864;    m.   Edward B. Nevin.
He commenced life  as a teacher.             In 1849 he went to California in
the Edward Everett,   which ship,  the succeeding year,   he,   with others,
purchased and went in her to  Peru.         Returning home,   he went into
business as a manufacturer of boots,    and when the War of the Rebel-
lion broke out,    he was in the leather business in Boston.
Fired  by  patriotism,      he  soon  organized  a  company  among  his
friends and townspeople,   and on 25 Apr. 1861,   they became Co. H of
the  famous  12th  Mass.       Volunteers   (Fletcher  Webster  Regiment) .
Hewas elected captain,  and onJune 26they were mustered into United
States  service.           His regiment saw hard service,     and he was always
foremost in performance of his duty.        On 7 July,   1862,  he was made
provost marshal,   and 5 Aug. promoted to major,   to serve in the 33d
Mass.  Regiment.
After Colonel Webster was killed,  Major Bates was made colonel of
his old regiment,   the 12th  Massachusetts,   in Sept. 1862.    He was at
the headof his regiment in the battles of Fredericksburg,   Chancellors-
ville and Gettysburg and in the latter engagement,   1 July,    1863,     was
severely wounded in the neck,  but declined to leave his post.
OnJuly 24 he was detailed on recruiting service in Massachusetts,
having command of the conscript  camp at Gallup's Island,     Boston
Harbor,   returning to the seat of war on 28 Mar. 1864.
He commanded the 2d Brigade from 8 May,   1864,   to 25 June,    1864,
andwas mustered out with his regiment on 8 July,  1864.
He was afterward  brevetted as brigadier  general  for  meritorious
service.
After his  return  home,    he for  two years occupied the  position  of
cashier of First  National Bank of South Weymouth,  and then entered
thebanking business in Boston,  which he continued till his decease.
He was a charter member of Post 58,   G. A. R.,   was elected the first
commander,    and held that office during his life,  with the exception of
the year 1870,   when he was commander of the Department of Massa-
chusetts.
He was a man of dignified bearing and strict integrity,   beloved by
his  comrades,    and respected even by those against  whom he fought.
Even as late as  1899 he was remembered by Secessionists with whom
he came in contact during his military service,   and they voluntarily
testified to his kindness of heart and gentlemanly conduct.

BAYLEY
1.   REV.      JAMES   BAYLEY (James, 4 Rev. James,    John,       John¹) ,
son of James and Elizabeth (Ruggles) Bayley,  was born at Roxbury,
22 Mar.  1697-98;     died  at  Weymouth,   22 Aug.  1766,     in  the  69th
year of his age.       He graduated at Harvard College in  1719 and was
ordained minister of the Second Parish of Weymouth,  26 Sept.  1723.
He was a schoolmaster at Andover in 1721.    He married,   before 26
Feb.  1721-22,     Sarah      , who survived her husband.
James Bayley of Weymouth,   clerk,  made his will 9 June,     1766,    as
follows:   To his  wife  Sarah the use  of  his  estate for  life.     To  sons
James,        Joshua,       Thomas,     Nathaniel  and John what  remains  after
their   mother's  decease,      equally.        Having  already  given  his   two
daughters Sarah and Mary £26 6s.    4d.    each,   my wife to dispose of
what gold and silver as she pleases to them.       My wife to dispose of
my Library equally among her children,  excepting Pool's Annotations,
which I give to my son James.        My wife with sons James and Na-
thaniel   to  be  executors.          Witnesses:         Joseph  Vining,        Benjamin
Vining,        Jr. ,       and  Ruth  Torrey.       Probated  19 Sept.  1766  (Suffolk
Probate Records,   65:    364),  and administration granted to the three
executors.            Joshua  Bayley  and John  Bayley,   gentlemen,     both  of
Woolwich,    Me. ,  released unto Thomas Bayley of Boston,   gentleman,
all  rights  in the estate  of their  late  father,     James Bayley,     late  of
Weymouth,  clerk,   for  £6 13s.  4d.,   1 June,  1774.    (Ibid.      73 :    709.)
Children,   born at Weymouth except the first:
James,         b.       15 Jan.  1721-22;    bp.    at Andover,     1721 .
Sarah,     b.      27 Apr.  1724;    d.     7 Apr.  1733.
Elizabeth,      b.     22 July,    1725;      d.    July,    1725.

BENT
REV.        JOSIAH  BENT  (Josiah,       John,         Ebenezer,         Joshua,         Jo-
seph,        John¹)  was born at Milton,    1 Oct. 1797;   died at Amherst,      19
Nov.  1839.    He graduated at Harvard College 1822,    studied for  the
ministry  and  was  ordained  minister  of  the  First  Parish  of  Wey-
mouth,      13 Oct.  1824.    He served till  10 Oct.  1833.    He delivered
an historical address  at  Weymouth,   28 Nov.  1832,   which was pub-
lished.              Later  he  served  as  minister  at  Falmouth  and  Amherst.
He married at Albany,    N.  Y.,     25  Oct.  1824,     Paulina Rice,    daugh-
ter of Ithamar and Sarah (Dunn)  Rice.        She was born at Sudbury,
24 Feb.  1800,     and died at Springfield,  11 July,    1889.

BERNARD  (BARNARD)
1.   REV.           RICHARD    BERNARD,    son   of   John   Bernard   of
Epworth  in  Linconshire,      was  born  in   1567;      died  at  Batcombe,
Somersetshire,   in  Mar. 1641.    He graduated at Christ's College,  Cam-
bridge,     in  1594-95;     was vicar of Worksop,   Nottinghamshire,   1601 to
1613-14;    rector  of  Batcombe,     Somersetshire,      1613  to   1641.     He
was  a  conformable  Puritan,     but  was  opposed  to  total  separation
from the Established Church.
In  October,        1638,       in  his  History  of  New England,     Gov.  John
Winthrop wrote:      "About two years since  [1635]   one Mr.  Bernard,
a minister  of  Batcombe in  Somersetshire  in England,    sent  over  two
books  in  writing,     one  to  the  magistrates,       and the  other  to  the  elders ,
wherein he laid down arguments against the manner of our gathering
our churches,    etc.  which the elders  could  not answer till  this  time
[1638] ,     by  reason  of  the  many troubles  about  Mrs.  Hutchinson's
opinions,   etc."
In closing  his  account  of the troubles  at  Weymouth with  Rev.
Robert  Lenthall,     Winthrop associates  Mr. Bernard's book with the
troubles  there.           He said :       " One Britton,     who had spoken reproach-
fully of the answer,    which was sent to Mr. Barnard his  book against
our church covenant and some of the elders "  was convicted by the
General  Court.
In  1736  Prince  first  published  his  Chronological  History  of New
England,     and there  the statement  first  appears  in  print  that  there
was at  Weymouth early  one Rev.  Mr.  Bernard.        Prince  adds:      " I
do not anywhere find  the least  hint of him,   except  in a letter  from
some of the oldest people at  Weymouth.   "
 - 81 - 
BERNARD                                  77
It was the connection of Rev. Richard Bernard's  books  with the
church troubles at Weymouth in 1638 that led to the introduction
of a Rev.  Mr. Bernard as their first  non-conformist minister there.
Only fragments of the parish register of Batcombe have been pre-
served.              These  have  been  published  from  copies  of  the  Bishop's
Transcripts at Wells,     recently.           They contain a few baptisms,      mar-
riages  and burials  for  the years  1597,     1605,      1607,     1608,    1616,     1617,
1629,      1662 and  1669.    The transcripts  for  the years 1617 and 1629
are signed  " Richard Bernard,   rector. "    No item relating to any other
person named Bernard is  found among these fragments.             He was the
author of several  books,    one of which was entitled,   Plain Evidence :
the Church of England is Apostolicall,  the Separation Schismaticall.

2.   MASAKIELL   BERNARD,   son  of  Rev.  Richard  Bernard  of
Worksop,      Nottinghamshire,     and of Batcombe,     Somersetshire,      was
baptized at Worksop,   27 Sept.  1607.
Massachiel  Bernard,    aged 24 yeare,   Mary Barnard his wife aged
28 yeare,      John  Bernard  his  sonne aged 3 yeare and Nathaniel  his
sonne aged one yeare came from Batcombe in Somersetshire in Rev.
Joseph Hull's Company,  sailing  from Weymouth,    Dorsetshire,    on or
near  20 Mar.  1634-35.             The town of  Weymouth granted him two
lots " in the plaine" and one " in the mill field."   He also had one of
the great lot  " on the  East  side  of  Fresh Pond" granted to him,   2
Feb.  1651-52.           He is  not named among the grantees of Weymouth,
14  Dec.   1663.     (Weymouth  Land  Grants,     273,        281-283) .               He
was called a clothier in 1634,   and was fined for giving "strong water"
to  Henry  Allein  and  Clement  Weaver,      "persons  at  work  at  his
house, "  2 June,   1640.    (Massachusetts Bay Colony Records,   1:   297.)
His Christian name is  found spelled Maschil,    Masachell,     Masakiell,
Masachet and Musachiel.
Children,    first two born in England,  last two in Weymouth:
John,       b.   near 1631 .
Nathaniel,     b.    near 1633.
Mary,     b.     27 Sept.  1637.
Sarah,    b.     5 Apr.  1639.
RICHARD  BARNARD was one of the Weymouth men who took
the oath of allegiance  to  His Majesty in  1678-79.           He is  probably
the  Boston  man whom Savage says  died  in  Dec.  1706.    (Savage's
Genealogical Dictionary,   1:   120.)

BLACKSTONE  (BLAXTON)
'    REV.            WILLIAM   BLACKSTONE,       non-conformist,           came   to
Wessagusset,     with the Robert Gorges Company,    arriving about the
middle of September,  1623.    He matriculated as a sizar at Emman-
uel  College,    Cambridge,    at the Easter term,    1614;  graduated A.B.
in  1617-18;     and obtained  the  degree A.M.  in  1621.    He was  born
near  1595  in  England,    son of John and Agnes  (Hawley)   Blaxton,
was baptized at Horncastle,   Lincolnshire,   5 Mar.  1595-96.              (Regis-
ter  of Horncastle,   1:27.)     It is  stated that he took his  first  degree
at Emmanuel College,   Cambridge,   in  1617 and his second degree in
1623.     (Bostonian  Society  Publication,     Second  Series,    2:73.  )     The
Matriculations  and  Degrees,       University  of  Cambridge,      show  that
he  received A.B.  in  1617-18 and A.M. from Emmanuel College  in
1621.    He removed  from  Wessagusset  to  Shawmut  (now Boston)
near  1625,         and died  at  Rehoboth,     and  was buried there  28 May,
1675.    He was the  first   white  inhabitant  of  what is  now Boston.
In Governor Bradford's letter to his Majesty's Council for New Eng-
land,      dated 9 June,   1628,    " Mr.  Blackston"  had contributed 12 shill-
ings  towards  the  charge  of sending Thomas  Morton back to Eng-
land.         He was appointed by John Gorges  to  put John  Oldham  in
possession  of  his  land,    21  Apr.  1629.    (Suffolk  County  Deeds,     1:
xiii. )     He  was   named  by   Sir    Ferdinando   Gorges   as   one   of
the grantees of land in Maine in Dec.,   1631.    On 10 Feb. 1631,   Gov-
ernor  Winthrop  wrote  in  his  journal  that  "it  hath  been  observed
ever since  this  bay was planted  by  Englishmen,      viz. ,     seven  years ,
that at this day the frost hath broken up every year. "     This chance
memorandum carries  us back to  10 Feb. 1624;  and as Blackstone
 - 101 - 
BLANCHARD                                97
was the only inhabitant of Shawmut when Winthrop and his people
arrived,       it   follows  that  he,    in  all  probability,     learned  about  the
weather from Blackstone,    a student and an observer.
"Mr.  Willm  Blackestone"  is  named as third on the list  of  those
who took the oath of freemen in the Massachusetts Bay Colony,   18
May,     1631.    In writing  about the Gorges  Company of  1623,      Gov-
ernor  William  Bradford  stated  in his  History  of  Plymouth  Plan-
tation (Edition of 1912,   1:  337)  that some of the Gorges  Company
"went for  England,   others  for  Virginia,    some few remained and were
helped with supplies from hence. "    It is  evident that the first white
inhabitant  of  Shawmut  was  one  who  remained.
He was a clergyman of the Established Church,   and disposed of
his  lands in Boston and "went from Boston,    having lived there nine
or ten years," as Lechford tells us,  to Rhode Island.         This  removal
took place in the spring of 1635.    He settled in Cumberland (now
Lonsdale),     and was the first  white settler  to permanently locate  in
that State,   then considered to be in ancient Rehoboth in  Plymouth
Colony.
Mr.  William Blackston and Sarah Stevenson,    widow of John Ste-
venson  of  Boston,    were married in Boston,   4 July,   1659,      by Gov.
John Endicott.            (Boston Vital  Records,   1630-99,      p.       71.)       Sarah,
the wife of William  Blackstone,    was buried at Rehoboth about the
middle  of  June,     1673.    (Proceedings  of  Massachusetts  Historical
Society,    1878,    pp.     194-206. )
• Child:
John;   sold  the land  inherited  from his  father  and removed  to
Providence in 1692.
BLANCHARD
1.   THOMAS  BLANCHARD came from the vicinity of Andover,
county  of  Hants,      England,    to  New England.        He married  at  St.
Edmunds,      Salisbury,    Wiltshire,    15 May,   1637,    widow Ann Barnes
of  St.   Edmunds.       (The  Genealogist,    N.   S.   30:  123.)    His  licence
calls him yeoman and widower,  of Clatford,  county of Southampton,
a parish two miles south of Andover.      Ann Barnes was the widow
of  Richard Barnes and the daughter of Robert and Agnes (Gosling)
Bent  of   Penton-Grafton,     county  of  Hampshire.      She  was  bap-
tized  there  16  July,     1602.    With  her  second  husband,      Thomas
Blanchard,     she sailed from London,   in the ship Jonathan,     for  New
England 12 Apr.  1639,   and died on the voyage.       (Bent Genealogy,
10.)      Upon reaching  New England  Thomas  Blanchard  settled,     in
1639,       in Braintree,   but removed to  Charlestown in 1651.    His first
wife's  name does  not appear to  be known.           After  arriving  in  New
England,     he married (3)  Mary     , who survived  him.          He made
his  will  22 May,    1654,    and it  was proved 20 June,    1654.     (Ν.      Ε.
H. G. S.  Register,  17:  156;  32:   407-411.)

1.   RICHARD¹  BOLTER of  Weymouth was made a freeman  18
May,       1653,      and another  Richard Boulter  was  made a freeman  23
May,     1655.    The inventory of the estate of Thomas Streame,     late of
Weymouth,    taken 1 July,  1662,    mentions  "12 acres of upland neare
Richd  Bolters   house. "     (Register,    11:   173.)    In  1662  "Goodman"
Bolter,     Sr. ,    from Weymouth had one of the twenty-three allotments
of land  in  Mendon,    and at the same time Tho.  Bolter  from Wey-
mouth had another  allotment  there  (Ibid.        9 :     51),   on  condition  that
they  settle  at  "Nipmugg"  (Mendon)  before  the end of Sept.  1663.
He received,     however,   6 acres  in the First Division and 18 acres  in
the Second Division,  in Weymouth,  14 Dec. 1663.    (Weymouth Land
Grants,   283.)
Administration on the estate of Richard Bolter,  late of Weymouth,
deceased,   was granted unto Thomas Bolter,  "his son," 25 Mar. 1679.
The inventory was taken by Thomas Dunn and Jacob Nash,   1 Mar.
1678-79.                      (Suffolk  Probate Records,    12:   279.)

BRANDON
WILLIAM   BRANDON came from  Ashton  Clinton,     county  of
Bucks,  England,   to Weymouth.         His land in Weymouth was bounded
by the lands of John Taylor,   John Staples,    Simon Whitmarsh and
Thomas Richards.      Land was granted in his name 3 Feb.  1651.
16 Nov. 1647,    Mary Branden,   widow of William Branden,    late of
Ashton Clinton,    in county  of Buckingham,    doth constitute Richard
Baldwin  of  Milford,    Conn.,   her attorney  to  receive  an account  of
Wm.     Branden  and  Thomas  Branden,      sons  of  Thomas  Branden  of
Putnam,      county of Hertford,     yeoman,    for  a messuage and lands in
Ashton Clinton by vertue of her husband's last  will.         (Aspinwall's
Notarial Records,     104.)
Following marriages are taken from Ashton Clinton  parish  regis-
ters:   John Wells and Sarah Branden,    married  29 July,    1621.    Wm.
Bampton and Martha Branden,   married 19 July,  1627.    Christopher
Welles and Joane Brandon,   married 12 May,   1636.
He made his  will 31 Aug.  1646,   as follows:    To his  wife Mary he
gave his dwelling and land adjoining;  to  his  son Thomas land "by
the  mill  path,"  his  two  guns,      musket  and fowling  piece;    to  his
daughter Sarah a cow at the age of 13 years;    to  his daughter Mary
a cow at same age,  and likewise to his daughter Hannah;    to  his son
Thomas his  houses  and lands,    one-half  at the age of  21  years,     the
other half to his wife,    she saving £15 out ofit to his three daughters
when  they come  to   16  years,        each  £5.           If  his  son  Thomas die
before he comes of age,   he gives  to his  brother  William,    his  eldest
son,       £10.               Approved on testimony of Edward Bates,    28 Oct.  1647.
(Register,   7:     172.)
Children:
Thomas,         alive 31 Aug. 1646.
Sarah,    under 13 yrs.,   31 Aug. 1646.
Mary,   under 13 yrs.  31 Aug.  1646;    m.    11  Nov. 1659,   James Smith
ofWeymouth.
Hannah,    d.    at Weymouth,   9 Oct.  1662.

BRIGGS  (BRIGGES)
of
CLEMENT BRIGGS,  a felmonger,   came from Southwark,    county
of Surrey,    England,    to  Plymouth in the  Fortune,    arriving at Plym-
outh,     11  Nov.  1621.    He received  a grant  of  land  at  Plymouth,
as  one "which came  in  the  Fortune"  in Mar.  1623,     being  one
thirty-five  persons  who came in that ship.       He did not long remain
at Plymouth,    for on 1 Mar. 1630-31,    the General Court of the Massa-
chusetts  Bay  Colony  "ffyned"   Mr.  Tho :      Stoughton,      constable  of
Dorchester,     for  taking  upon him to  marry Clemt Briggs and Joane
Allen.            (Records of  Massachusetts  Bay Colony,   1:83. )      This shows
that  they  were  married  probably  at  Dorchester  shortly  before,      1
Mar.  1630-31.            He  entertained  an  Indian  "without  leave"  of  the
Court,    for  which  he was  fined  ten shillings,   4 Sept.  1634.     (Ibid.
132.)
"The  deposition  of   Clement  Briggs  of   Weymouth,      felmonger,
taken at  New Plymouth the  29 day of August  ...  1638,    before
Thom Prence  of  New Plymouth,   gent.    Govt.     and Willm.       Bradford
of the same Gent,   assistant of the govat &c.
..
"This  Deponent          sayeth  that  about  two  and  twenty  years
since  [near  1616] ,     this  depont  then  dwelling  wth   Mr.  Samuel  La-
thame  in  Barmundsey  street,       Southwarke,      felmonger,       and  one
Thomas Harlow then also  dwelling  wth  Mr. Robte Heeks [Hicks  who
came in  the  Fortune]     in  the  same street  a felmonger          where
they worked 'for the space of  three or four yeares. ' "
land Historical and Genealogical Register,    2:  244.)
(New Eng-
He had 10 acres  granted  to  him  "on the  Easter  neck,"  2 acres
"upon the neck at the fferry " and 2   acres "at  Hocklie.  "     Lot No. 9
on the east side of Fresh Pond was granted to his name 2 Feb.  1651-
52.     He made his  will  in 1648,    and it  was probated 24 Oct.  1650.
To  his  son  Thomas he  gave  his  home lot  at  Plymouth;     to  his  son
Jonathan land joining to John Rees land at 18 years,    and at 21 years
one-fourth of all his land in Weymouth;    to his son Clement his  hous-
ing and one-half of his  land in Weymouth,    at 21 years of age,     if  his
mother be deceased before or after her decease;   to his  sons Thomas,
David,    John and Remember ( ?)  his other land at Plymouth equally,
Clement to give his brother Remember 20s.   and John 10s.   and Jona-
than to give  his  brother  David 10s.    and to  brother  Thomas  10s.
Witnesses:     John Rogers  and Robert  Tucker.        Testified  to  24 Oct.
1650.     (Suffolk  Probate,    N.  S. ,     1 :  456.)

BRITTON
JAMES  BRITTON had land granted to him early at Weymouth.
It  was bounded on the east  by Clement Brigg's "ten acres  in  the
Easter  neck. "    He also  had a lot  laid  out on the east  side  of the
Great  Pond,      3  Feb.  1651.    He was  punished  for  causing  trouble
for  Mr. Robert  Lenthall and the church at Weymouth,   by the Gen-
eral Court,      13 Mar. 1638-39.            ( Massachusetts Bay Records,    1:  254.)
The church had then been organized only about six weeks.        Awrong
done him was acknowledged 2 June,  1640.    He removed to Woburn
in that year.             He was ill  affected,  both to our  church government
and civil  government,   and was executed for the crime of adultery in
1643.     (Winthrop's History  of  New England,    2 :    191,    192.)

BROWN -BURGE
BROWN
131
RICHARD  BROWN,   son  of  Thomas and Joan Brown of  Swan
Hall,      Hawkedon,   county of Suffolk,   England,   was born  near  1575 ;
settled  first   in  London,   where  he was ruling  elder  in  a church  of
Separatists ;     was one of  the earliest  settlers  of  Watertown,    and the
first   Ruling  Elder  of  the  church  there  organized.        He desired  to
become a  freeman  in  Oct.   1630,     and  was  made a freeman of  the
Massachusetts Bay Colony,    18 May,    1631.    He was removed from
his office  in  the Watertown  Church for  heretical  opinions  in  1632.
Hemade a complaint when the red cross was cut out of the ensign at
Salem,    5 Nov.  1634.    He was a man of influence,    a  selectman  for
several  years,    and a representative  from  Watertown from  1634  to
1657;    a  commissioner  "to  end small causes, "  1638  to  1656.    On 2
Dec. 1657,     he purchased of  Humphrey and Rebecca  Booth a house
in Charlestown to  which he removed.       He then called himself 81  or
82 years of age.
He married  at  Weymouth,  -probably a second  marriage,  -in
Nov.  1648,     Elizabeth  Marsh,    widow of George Marsh of Hingham.
The foregoing marriage is  recorded  in  Rev.  Peter  Hobart's  Diary.
He died at Charlestown between 6 Aug. 1659,  and 20 Mar. 1660-61.
He made his will on the 6 Aug. 1659,   making his wife Elizabeth sole
executrix,      his  son  Thomas  Brown and his  grandsons  Richard and
George to have small sums,    if they personally appear in this  land to
demand the same,    and not  otherwise.         Jonathan  Simpson to  have
20s.      if  he serve faithfully;  Phinehas Pratt  to have a suit of clothes.
His wife to have £20 besides her own goods which she brought to him.
Inventory taken 6 Oct.  1660,     £249 13s.          His widow married (3)   12
May,     1662,   Richard Jackson of Cambridge.      She died 11 Jan.  1676-
77.     Lincoln,      in  his  Hingham Genealogies,    says  she  married  (2)   in
Nov.  1648,      Richard  Bowen,    but this  is  an error  for  Brown.            The
marriage  occurred at Weymouth.
BURGE
JOHN  BURGE had land which was first  granted to Massacheill
Barnard,       granted  to  him  in  "Harrises  Rainge,"  about  1643.    He
also had other lots  granted to him in the First and Second Divisions
of Weymouth,    14 Dec.  1663.    (Weymouth Land Grants,      256,      282,
284.)     He made a deposition concerning the estate  of William Fry
of Weymouth,    9  Nov.  1643.    (Register,   2:  385.)     "Rebecca  -,
the wife of John Burge died at Weymouth,    1 May,   1661."     (Suffolk
County Returns, Boston City Registrar's office, p.  482.)    About 1662
he removed to Chelmsford.        John Burge, "late of Weymouth, "  mar-
ried (2)  at Chelmsford,  9 June,  1662,   Mary (Stearns)  Larned,   widow
of Isaac Larned of Chelmsford,   daughter of Isaac Stearns,    baptized
in Nayland,   county of Suffolk,  26 Jan.  1626.    She died at Chelms-
ford,     8 or 9 Jan.  1663.    He married (3)  at Chelmsford,   3 July,   1667,
widow Grisell  Gurney,    he  being  her  fifth  husband.       She  died  at
Chelmsford,       9 July,    1669.    He married  (4)  at Chelmsford,    6 Sept.

1677,      Jane Gurney, widow of John Gurney (Gurnells) of Dorchester.
She died at Dorchester,  4 Apr. 1678,  and he died there 22 Oct.  1678.

BURSLEY
JOHN  BURSLEY (Burslem,     Burslym,    Burslynn)  came with the
Gorges  Company to  Wessagusset  about  the middle of Sept.  1623.
Governor  William  Bradford,    in  his  letter  to  his  Majesty's  Council
for  New England,   dated 9 June,   1628,   sets  forth  that  "some of the
chief of every plantation" had subscribed towards the charge of send-
ing back to England Mr. Thomas Morton.           He reported the planta-
tions as follows :
From Plymouth
From Naumkeak [Salem]
From Pascataquack [Little Harbor in  Portsmouth,    N. H.]
From Mr. Jeffrey  and Mr. Burslem [Wessagusset]
From Natascot [Hull]
From Mr. Blackton [Boston]
From Edward Hilton [Dover Point,    N. H.]
From Mrs. Thompson [Thompson's Island,  Boston Harbor]

(Collections of the Massachusetts Historical Society,   1794,   Vol.   3 :   63.)
Therefore,         Mr.  Jeffrey  (which  see)   and  Mr.  Burslem  were  con-
sidered  by  Governor  Bradford to be chief men of one of  the  eight
plantations of New England,    9 June,    1628,    and the Cape Ann plan-
tation,   if then in existence,  was not mentioned.          "Mr. John Burslin"
desired to  be made a  freeman  19 Oct.  1630,    and "Mr. Jo.     Burslyn"
took the freeman's oath in the Massachusetts  Bay Colony,    18 May,
1631.     (Register,    3 :    90,    91.)
The Records of the Massachusetts Bay Colony,  under the date of
3 June,    1634,    read as follows :
"Whereas  Thomas Lane,   late  servt  to John Burslyn,   by the pvi-
dence of God,   is  fallen lame & impotent,   &hath since remayned att
Dorchest ,      where hee hath bene chargeable to that plantačon,    & like
soe to contynue,  it is therefore ordered,   that the inhabitants of Wes-
saguscus  shall  send to  Dorchester for  the said Thomas Lane & shall
pay for all the charges they have beene att  in keepeing  him dureing
his  aboade att   Dorchest . "     ( Massachusetts  Bay Colony  Records,
1:  121.)
He married,     about 28 Nov.  1639,   Joanna Hull,   daughter of Rev.
Joseph Hull of Weymouth (1635-39),  and removed to Sandwich and
Barnstable,    where his subsequent history is  to be found.
BUTTERWORTH
Henry,        John,      Mary  and  Samuel  Butterworth  were  residing   in
Weymouth before  1635.
HENRY  BUTTERWORTH died at Weymouth between 7 June,
1635,     and Apr. 1645.    The inventory of his estate,   "as far as can be
remembered, "  was  taken  by  Edward Bates,    Richard Adams  and
 - 152 - 
148                                      BUTTERWORTH
William  Carpenter,     in which  they  state  that  "he deceased  in  the
winter 4 years since, "  and refer  to  woolen and linen  "the Children
have worne out."    This  inventory is  undated,    but Richard  Adams
resided  in  Weymouth from 7 June,    1635,   to  shortly before  10 Apr.
1649,    when he was living in Malden.          Undoubtedly the Widow But-
terworth,       who had a great  lot  granted  to  her  on the east  side  of
"Fresh  Pond, "  26 Feb.  1651,     was  his  widow.          (Weymouth  Land
Grants,      281.)      His widow may be the Mary Butterworth who mar-
ried Sampson Mason of Rehoboth,   but proof of  this  statement  has
not been found.
MARY  BUTTERWORTH (see Clifton) .
JOHN  BUTTERWORTH resided  at  Weymouth  from  1635  to
1644,     "nine or ten years. "     He was a  "brother"  to  Samuel Butter-
worth,    and the  two occupied the same lot  and probably  the  same
house at  Weymouth for  "nine  or  ten years.  "     He was  propounded
to take up his  freedom in the Plymouth Colony,  4 May,    1652,      and
again,          8   June,        1655,       and  still   again,       6  June,       1660.    (Plymouth
Colony Records,    3 :    8,     78,     188.)     He was a constable  of  Rehoboth
in 1660.    He was one of five to have charge of admitting inhabitants
into  Wannamoisett (Swansey),   5 Mar.  1667-68 .            (Ibid.     4:     175-176. )
He removed to  Swansea and died at Bristol,   R. I.,    shortly before  1
Sept.  1708.     He married,    near  1650,     Sarah      .  Sampson Mason
of Rehoboth called John Butterworth  "his  brother, "  22  Oct.  1672,
and Plymouth Court deputed Mary Mason's "brother Butterworth"
to assist her in settling her husband's estate,   1 Nov. 1676.    The First
Baptist Church of Swansea was organized at his house in  1663.     The
names of his sixth,   seventh,  eighth and ninth children are illegible  on
Rehoboth  town records,    but  they were born  8 Sept.  1661,      22  Jan.
1663,      Mar.  1665,    and May,   1667.    (See New England Historical and
Genealogical  Register,    41:  191,    192.)
Children,   born at Rehoboth:

SAMUEL  BUTTERWORTH was  born  near  1610,    and came to
Charlestown early.       He purchased of Robert Jeffery a small house and
six acres at Weymouth, about 1635.    Let his deposition tell the story.
 - 153 - 
BYRAM                                 149
DEPOSITION.
I  Samuel Butterworth aged about 56 years testifyeth  and saith
that about 34 yrs.    since  when I  had been but a little  while  in  this
country  I  lived at  Charlestown and then  I meet with a man whoose
[name]   was Robt Jeffery  and I heard that he had a little  house and
land at  Waymoth and I  bought  it  for  I  and my brother ;    and the
land adjoyning  to  the house was six  acres and the price of all  was
five pound and my brother and sister did Injoy two thirds of it  until
they went to Seconke [Rehoboth]   which was about nine or ten years
and then we sold  it  againe          to  Henry Kingman,                                  deposed
in  Court, "   26  July  1665.    (Suffolk  Court  Files,    815,    16th paper.)
He also desposed  "yt ye home lott yt was first given to Robert Jeffery
es in Waymouth about 31 years since was six acres, " and that it was
"nere a place  there  called  King oake  hill, "   2  Nov.  1666.     (Ibid.
14th paper. )
...
...
He was  made a freeman of  the  Massachusetts  Bay  Colony,      13
May,    1640,   and had lot  26 in the great lots on the east side of " Fresh
Pond"  granted to him 26 Feb.  1651.    He also  had six acres  in the
First  Division and  eighteen  acres  in  the  Second  Division  granted
him,    14 Dec.  1663.    (Weymouth Land Grants,   281,   282,     283.)      He
was one of the first  purchasers of Rehoboth,   and had a £50 alottment
there about  1643,    and drew lot  No.  12 at a  town meeting 30 June,
1644.    He drew lot  14 "for  the great plain"  9 June,   1645.    He was
buried at  Rehoboth,   1 Sept.  1685.    He made his  will 13 Oct.  1684,
and it  was proved 3 Mar. 1685-86.            In it  he mentions his  "cousins "
(nephews)  Abraham Butterworth of Rhode Island,  John Butterworth
of  Swansea,      William  Hayward of Swansea,   his  cousin  John Butter-
worth's  two  sons  Samuel and Benjamin,    his  cousin  Mary Mason,
widow of Sampson Mason of Swansea,   her  two sons Noah and Sam-
uel  Mason,     and his cousin Ann Butterworth,   daughter of Abraham.
His  cousin  John  Butterworth  of  Rehoboth  executor.         (Register,
41:  191.)    No mention at  Weymouth or Rehoboth has been found
of a wife or  children.

Although John Canterbury owned 74 acres  of land in Weymouth

herited  from his wife's family.       Joseph W. Porter said in  1892 that
John Canterbury's wife was the widow of John Vinson of Weymouth,
who died 20 Sept. 1718,  but he also says that she died 9 Dec.  1729,
(Register,   46:  188),  a statement which is not true.

CARPENTER
1.   WILLIAM¹   CARPENTER,    born  near  1576,     his  son  William
Carpenter,       Jr. ,     born  near  1605;    the  son's  wife  Abigail,     born  near
1606,      with their four  children,   the eldest born near 1628,    settled  in
Weymouth.              The senior  William  Carpenter was made a freeman of
the Massachusetts  Bay Colony,     13 May,    1640.    He was a deputy
from Weymouth in  1641  and  1643.    He removed  to  Rehoboth  in
1644.    He made his  will  10 Dec.  1658,     and it  was proved 21 Apr.
1659.     To his sons John,   William,   Joseph,   and to his daughter Han-
nah,   to his son Abiah,   to his daughter Abigail,   to his son-in-law John
Titus,   to his son Samuel and to his wife not named,   he made bequests.
"William  Carpenter,    aged 62 years,     William Carpenter,      Jr. ,      aged
33 years,     carpenters,      of  Horwell,     Abigail  Carpenter  aged 32  years
and fower children ten years and under"  sailed for  New England in
the ship Bevis of 150 tons,   Robert Batten master,   from Southampton,
Eng. ,     before  2  May,      1638.    (Hotten's  Original  Lists  of  Emigrants,
1600-1700,       pp.      298-299;    Drake's  Founders  of  New England,       60.)
Wherwell  is  a parish about  three and one-half  miles southeast  from
Andover in Hants.

CHAPMAN
CHAPMAN,   a  Londoner,    came in  the Gorges  Company to
Wessagussett  in Sept.  1623.    He brought  £80 worth  of  provisions
and  two  servants.               He died   in   five   months   after   he   arrived
in New England.        (Leavett's  Voyage in  1623-24,    published in  Col-
lections  of  the  Massachusetts  Historical  Society,     Third  Series,       8 :
158-190. )     His must have been one of the earliest  deaths  in Wey-
mouth.

CHURCH -CLAPP
CHURCH
159
RICHARD  CHURCH,   "a sojourner "  removed from  "Wessagass-
cusett" to Plymouth before 6 Feb. 1631-32.       He desired to be made
a freeman  of  the  Massachusetts  Bay Colony,     19  Oct.   1630.    His
name  is   given  with  John  Taylor,      Richard  Silvester,       and  Robert
Abell,  all of whom were early settlers at Wessagussett.        It cannot be
doubted that he was then living  there.
Gov.  William  Bradford  wrote  a letter  from  Plymouth,     6 Feb.
1631-32,        to  Gov.  John  Winthrop,     in  which  he said  among other
things:
"Richard  Church  came  likewise  as  a soujourner  to  work for  ye
present;   though he is  still  here residente  longer  than he purposed.
And what he will doe,   neither we nor I  thinke himselfe knowes;    but
if he resolve here to setle we shall require of him to procure a dismis-
ion;  but he did affirme to us at ye first  that he was one of Mr. [  -]
Webb's  men  and freed  to  goe  for  England or whither  he would,    ye
wch  we ye  rather  beleved  because  he came to  us  from  Wessagass-
cusett  upon ye falling  out with  his  partner. "     (The Mayflower De-
scendant,    9 :    3.)
This letter  implies that  Richard Church was neither a member of
those who came in Winthrop's fleet  in  1630,   nor of the Pilgrims  who
came to  Plymouth  in  the  Mayflower or  the  Fortune  in  1621.    He
was " one of  Mr. Webb's men. "
He evidently  settled  in Plymouth,  as he was taxed there  £1  16s.
on  2 Jan.  1632-33,     and again  £1  7s.   on 2 Jan.  1633-34.             He was
among the Plymouth men able to bear arms in Aug. 1643.    (Register,
4:   253,      254,      256.)     He was  made a  freeman of  Plymouth  Colony,
4 Oct.  1632.
It  has been stated that he came in Winthrop's fleet  in 1630,    but
that  appears  to  be  pure  supposition.          In view of the fact  that  he
was one of Mr. Webb's men and a sojourner,   according to Bradford,
it   is  probable  that he came before  1630 to  Wessagusset,     where he
first   appears.             According  to  his  deposition  made at  Sandwich  25
Aug.  1664,     he was  " aged about  56 yeares. "     (The  Mayflower  De-
scendant,   4:    152.)   Hence he was born near 1608 and died at Dedham,
27 Dec.  1668.    He resided in  Plymouth,    Eastham and Charlestown,
and from 1653 to  1668 at Hingham.          He married,    about 1636,   Eliza-
beth  Warren,    daughter  of  Richard  and  Elizabeth  Warren.        Her
father  was a  Mayflower  passenger.        She died at Hingham,     9 Mar.
1669-70.                       (For  their  twelve  children  see  Lincoln's  Genealogies  of
Hingham,     2 :      125,    and The Mayflower Descendant,   5:   118.)

CLIFTON
THOMAS  CLIFTON is  earliest  mentioned  in the Massachusetts
Bay Colony  Records  on  18  Jan.  1640-41,    as  follows:      " Mr.  James
Parker  is  alowed to  marry  Thomas  Clifton  & Mary Butterworth
within a month. "    ( Massachusetts Bay Colony Records,  1:  313.)   It
does not state  that these  were Weymouth people,  but Rev.  James
Parker  sold a house  and lands at  Weymouth,   26 Nov.  1644,     and
Thomas Clifton had six acres of land granted to him in the " west
field "  and two acres " in Harrises Rainge first given to Samuel Butter-
worth. "    He was made a freeman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony,
2 June,     1641,     and of Plymouth Colony,  7 June,  1648.   His wife was
probably  a  sister  to  John and Samuel Butterworth.       At a town
meeting,     30 June,   1644,   Thomas Clifton drew lot  48 at Rehoboth.
Hedrew lot 19there 9June, 1645,  and lot No. 5 in the "new meadow "
there  18 Feb.  1646.    No vital  records  of this  family are  found at
Weymouth nor  at  Rehoboth.        Savage says  he removed  to  Rhode
Island.

COLSON  (COLESON,     COLSTON)
1.   JOHN  COLSON was  born  near  1681 ;   died  at Weymouth,    4
July,     1752,      in his 71st year.          Mary Colson widow,  who died at Wey-
mouth,     8 Feb.  1715-16,    was undoubtedly  his  mother.          He married
at Hingham,     29 May,   1706,   Susannah Lincoln,   daughter of Thomas
and  Sarah  (Lewis)   Lincoln,     born at  Hingham,    19 Sept.  1688.    He
resided in Hingham till  1  Feb.  1711-12,    when he purchased "a house
and land at a place called Mutton Lane in Weymouth of John Por-
ter for  £140.  "     This property of 60 acres  he sold to Daniel  Cushing
of Hingham,      20 Aug.  1727.    (Suffolk  Deeds,     41 :   134.
By trade he was a glazier and made his will 3 May,    1749,   which was
proved 24 July,    1752.    To his  wife he gave the use of his estate for
life;    to his son  Thomas Colson,     £2;   to son Josiah  Colson,      £250;     to
son Ebenezer Colson,    £200;      to  his daughter Susannah Ager,   £2,   be-
sides what she hath already had;    to daughter Elizabeth  Hovey,      £2
on like  condition;    to  daughter Ann Shaw,     £2 likewise;   to  daughter
Sarah  Colson,       £150.             To his  grandson John Colson,    £5 at 21 ;    to his
grandson  Christopher  Colson,    £10 at 21 ;    to his  granddaughter Deb-
orah Colson,     £5 at 18.    At his wife's decease  his estate to be equally
divided amongst his three sons,    Thomas,    Ebenezer and Josiah,   Eben
 - 171 - 
COLSON                                     167
ezer  to  be executor.          Witnesses:   Micah White,     Thomas Blanchard,
Jr. ,    Samuel Blunt,   Jr.     (Suffolk Probate Records,  46: 425.)
His stone  standing  in  Pond  Plain  Cemetery,    South  Weymouth,
reads  as  follows:    "Here lies  buried Mr. John Colson who died July
4,    1752 in yº 71st year of his age. "
Col.  Thomas Vinson (1756-1841)  of Weymouth wrote an account
of his father's and mother's family in which he said:  "My grandfather
on my mother's side was John Colson.        He was born in the Island of
Bermuda in  the West Indies in the year 1681.    About ye year  1700
he came and settled in Weymouth near the Abington line.       About
1705  he  was  married  to   Susannah  Lincoln,     daughter  of  Thomas
Lincoln of Hingham.          Their children were five sons and six daugh-
ters,      viz.     John,     Thomas,     Ebenezer,      Brackley,   Josiah and Susannah,
Mary,       Elizabeth,     Anna and Sarah,   the  first.      She died  aged two.
Sarah,  the second, mymother,  was their youngest child.      John Colson,
the oldest,     married a Pettengill and had three children,   viz. ,     John,
Christopher  and Deborah.          He enlisted  as a soldier  in  the Indian
War and was killed about sunrise on a Sunday morning,   being a Sen-
tinel  on the walls of the Fort at Old York in Maine.      He was shot
by a skulking Indian,   the ball passing through his neck cutting the
life   vein.           He lived  about  two  hours.       Christopher  married  Ex-
perience White and had three children,  viz.,  Abiah,   Christopher and
Charity.       He left his family and his wife married Capt.     Moses Curtis
and  removed westward.         Deborah Colson  married  Joseph  Trufant
and had Susanna,   Joseph,   Colson,   Deborah,   James and John,   all re-
moving to Groton,  where the parents died."
Children,   first two born at Hingham,    others at Weymouth:

COOKE
WALTER  COOKE  received   four  acres   " in  the  Westerneck"
which had first  been granted  to  Thomas  " Baylie; "    also  an acте
" upon  Round Iland,"  first  granted  to  Thomas  Holbrook.            (Wey-
mouth Land Grants,  268.)     He received five  acres  in the First Di-
vision and fifteen acres in the Second Division,   14 Dec. 1663.    (Ibid.
282,        283.)      Walter Cooke of Weymouth was admitted a freeman of
the  Massachusetts  Bay Colony,    18  May,    1653.    (Register,     3:     192. )
How much earlier he came to New England is  a matter of conjecture.
He was one of twenty-three men from Braintree and from Weymouth
who accepted of allotments in Mendon in 1662 and agreed  to  settle
thereon before 30 Sept.  1663.    (Register,   9:51.)    He was a member
of the committee to build the minister's house at  Mendon,   2 Feb.
1669.    ( Ibid.      29:   182.)
His first  wife was Experience       , and his  second wife was Cath-
erine        , who died at  Mendon,    2 Jan.  1695-96.         He died there  5
Jan. 1695-96.
Walter  Cooke of Mendon,   being weak of body,   made his  will  18
Jan. 1694-95;    proved 5 Jan. 1697-98.            To his wife Catharine the use
of his estate.           John,  "being his eldest son," to have the great Bible
and ten acres;    son  Nicholas to have ten acres. "    Unto his children
Hannah,   Samuel,   Nicholas and Experience,  besides what he formerly
gave them,       the  reversion  of  his  movables after  his  wife's  decease.
Son John Cooke,   sole executor,   to whom administration was granted,
6 Jan.  1697-98.       (Suffolk  Probate Records,    8:   88.)
Children,   born at Weymouth:
John,     b.     near 1654.
Ebenezer,     b.      30 May,     1656.
Walter,    b.       10 Sept.  1657.
Nicholas,     b.       9 Feb.  1659-60;     settled  in Bellingham.

COOPER
JOHN  COOPER,  " a sojourner,   at the house of Henry Waltham
in Weymouth, "  made his will while residing there.       He desired  that
the wife  of  Henry  Waltham may be fully  satisfied  for  charges  in
"Phisicke, "  attendance,    etc. ,   and,   if any thing remains,    that Hazill-
penah Willocks (Hazelelponi Willix),  now resident  in Weymouth,    to
have 10s.               24 Feb. 1652-53.       He also  calls  Thos.     Dyer  his  " loving
friend.  "    This will  was proved by the deposition of William Torrey,
21  Oct.   1653.     Hazelelponi  Willix was the daughter  of  Balthazar
Willix  of  Exeter,      N.  H.    (Register,   68:81.)    It  is   apparent  that
John Cooper was without a family,  and probably only  temporarily
resided there.

CORNISH -COWING
CORNISH
177
RICHARD  CORNISH,  probably one of the Gorges Company,   was
an early  settler  of Weymouth.     He had lot  No.  16 granted  to  him
"on the East side of the fresh  pond next to  Mrs. Richards her mill. "
This  record was copied out of the "old  Towne book"  2  Feb.  1651,
and presented in Court in  1667.    (Suffolk Court Files,     815.)     At a
Court holden at Newe Towne (Cambridge),    5 Aug.  1634,     Richard
Cornish gave a bond of  £10 for  his "wyves"  personal appearance at
Court in  October following.            (Record of the Court of Assistants,    2 :
47.)    The record for  October does not show that she appeared,    but
at  a  Court holden at Cambridge,   5 June,    1638,   Katherine,    the wife
of Richard Cornish,   appeared and was fined.       Her fine was respited,
4 Dec.  1638.     (Ibid.       2:74,     79.)
Governor Winthrop,   under  the  date,     Feb.  1644-45,     says :     " One
Cornish,     dwelling some time in Weymouth,   removed to Acomenticus
(Agamenticus,   now York),   for  more outward accommodation,    and in
the last month was taken up in the river,  his head bruised and a pole
sticking in his side,  and his canoe laden with clay found sunk.  "   (Win-
throp's History,   2:  210.)    He was murdered,   and his  wife,    "being a
lewd woman,"  was tried for the murder,  convicted and executed.

DABYN
ROBERT  DABYN,   aged  28 years,    servant to  Rev. Joseph Hull,
sailed in Mr.  Hull's Company from Weymouth in Dorsetshire,    Eng.  ,
on or  near  20  Mar.  1634-35.           Mr. Hull came directly  from North-
leigh,     county  of  Devon,    to  Weymouth.           No later  reference  to  him
has been found.
DAGGETT  (DOGGETT)
THOMAS  DAGGETT was  born in England near  1607;   died  at
Marshfield,       18  Aug.  1692.    Thomas  "Doged, "  servant  to  Thomas
Oliver of Norwich,   county of Norfolk,  aged 30 years,   passed his exami-
nation "to passe for N. E. to inhabit," 13 May,   1637.    His first  wife,
whose  name is  unknown,    died at  Concord,    23 Aug.  1642.    He re-
moved to Weymouth and married (2),  about 1643,   Elizabeth (Hum-
phrey)    Frye,      widow  of  William  Frye and daughter  of  Jonas  and
Frances  (Cooley)    Humphrey,     who  came from  Wendover,   Bucking-
hamshire,    to  Dorchester,    as  early  as  1637.    She was probably bap-
tized at  Wendover,   and died at Weymouth near  1653.    He is  last
mentioned on Weymouth Town Records,    7 Mar. 1653.    His grant in
Weymouth was as follows :          " The Land of  Thomas Doget during the
life of his wife and afterwards to Elizabeth and Mary Frie the daugh-
ters  of  William  Frie  deceased, "   granted,     after  26 Oct.   1642,        four
acres "in the west field, " first  given to William Frie,   and twelve acres
"amongst the  greate lotes. "     (Weymouth Land Grants,     275,     280.)
He married  (3)  at  Marshfield,    17 Aug.  1654,    Joane Chillingsworth,
widow  of  Thomas  Chillingsworth,       whose  estate  was administered
upon,   in Mar.  1652-53.           She died at  Marshfield,   4 Sept.  1684.    Se-
lectman of Weymouth,    1648,     1651,    1652.
Childby first wife:
John,      b.    near 1642;    resided in Marshfield.
Children by second wife,   born at Weymouth:
Hannah,      b.       near  1646;   m.    24 June,   1673,     Samuel  Blanchard  of
Charlestown.

DERBY
1.   EDWARD¹ DERBY of Weymouth,   probably the son of Edward
and Susanna (Hooke)  Derby of Boston,   was born near  1665;   died at
Weymouth,   6 Jan. 1723-24.           He married (1),   near 1687,   Ruth Whit-
marsh,   daughter of Simon and Sarah (Holbrook)  Whitmarsh,    born at
Weymouth,     29 Sept.  1667;  she died near 1704.    He married  (2)  at
Hingham,       16  Oct.  1707,      Rebecca  (Sumner)   Hobart  of  Hingham,
widow of Aaron Hobart,   and daughter of Roger and Mary (Josselyn)
Sumner  of  Milton.         She  married  (3)  at  Braintree,    20  Dec.  1726,
Samuel Paine of Braintree.
He resided in both Weymouth and Braintree,  his first  child being
born in Weymouth,  his second being recorded inboth Weymouth and
Braintree,     the next four in Braintree,   and his seventh child at Wey-
mouth.             His  will   contains  the  following  essential  facts  (Register,
49: 340-341) :
Edward Derby,   "being sensible and apprehensive of the near ap-
proach of death,"  made his  will 4 Jan.  1723-24 as follows :      To his
wife Rebecca Derby part of his house and one-third of his income for
life.             His son Jonathan Derby to provide for  her.           His son Samuel
Derby to have a single share of his  estate,  as "he went from me at
 - 201 - 
DERBY                                  197
nineteen years of age and married. "    To his son Jonathan one-third
of his  "living  in  Weymouth. "    To his  daughter Sarah  Cobb  £40;
to daughter Jane Derby £50 and four silver  spoons that her mother
left.                To daughter Rebecca Derby £50;     to his daughter Ruth Derby
£50.               His land in Braintree to be sold to defray debts.           His unmar-
ried daughters to have their portions at 21 years of age or upon mar-
riage.        His wife Rebecca to  be executrix  and son Jonathan Derby
executor.             Witnesses:   John  Vinson,       John  Vining   and  Nathaniel
Symmes;    probated 13 Jan. 1723-24.            (Suffolk  Probate Records,     23:
101.)     Inventory taken 23 Jan. 1723-24,     £830 18s.     9d.

in Boston near 1796.    He married (intention at Weymouth,   26 Sept.

(Wade)  French,    baptized at the First  Church,    16 Aug.  1801;       she
died  there  9 Jan.  1894.    John¹  Dizer  occupied  a two-story wooden
dwelling  on  the  west  side  of  Peck's  Lane,    extending  from  Essex
Street  to Johonnet's  Wharf,    Boston,   in  1798.    There was a Francis
Dizer,       Sr. ,       who  married,    26 Feb.  1768,       Mary Hunt,    and a Mary
Dizer,     who married,    1 Oct.  1780,    Bartholomew York,      in Boston.

DRAKE
• 1.   THOMAS DRAKE first  appears  at Weymouth,   14 Dec.  1663.
Onthat day the town granted him six acres in the First Division and
eighteen acres  in the Second  Division.            (Weymouth Land Grants,
283.)     Hemarried (1) ,  near 1656, Jane Holbrook,  daughter of Thomas
and Jane Holbrook of  Weymouth.       She was called,    in the will  of
Thomas Holbrook,   dated 1 Dec. 1668,   "my daughter Jane Drake. "
She died near  1680.    He married  (2)  at  Marshfield,   9 Mar.  1681,
Millicent   (Ford)   Carver,    widow  of  John  Carver  of  Duxbury,     and
daughter  of  William  Ford,     who came to  Plymouth in the Fortune
in1621.
The author of Thomas Drake and Descendants,  published in 1896,
stated  that  he was the son  of  William  and Margaret  (Westover)
Drake,   born and baptized in the parish of Colyton,  county of Devon,
Eng. ,    13 Sept. 1635,  and that Elizabeth Drake,   who married in Bos-
ton,      8 June,      1654,     Ezekiel  Hamlin,   and Joane,  the wife  of  Thomas
Randall of Weymouth,   were his sisters .
William Drake,   a gentleman of Ash in the parish of Musbury,    was
licenced to marry Margaret Westover of the same place,   14 Nov. 1620.
(Exeter Marriage Licences,    p.    70.)     Musbury and Colyton are ad-
joining parishes.           The parish registers of Colyton call William Drake
a gentleman of the hamlet of Yarbury in Colyton.         They show the
following baptisms :
John Drake,    son of William of Yarbery,   bp.   24 Mar. 1621-22.
Dorothy  Drake,     daughter  of  William  of  Yarbery,     bp.       16 Mar.
1623-24.
Eleanor Drake,   daughter of William of Yarbery,  bp.   15 Dec. 1625.
Joane Drake,    daughter of William of Yarbery,  bp.  11 June,     1628.
William Drake,   son of William of Yarbery,   bp.    22 Dec. 1629.
Jane Drake,    daughter of William of Yarbery,  bp.   13 Feb. 1630-31.
Elizabeth Drake,   daughter of  William of Yarbery,  bp.   9 Dec. 1632.
Endimian Drake,    son of  William of Yarbery,   bp.   25 June,     1634.
Thomas Drake,    son of William of Yarbery,  bp.  13 Sept.  1635.
William Drake,   the father,   died 18 Nov. 1636,   and was buried in the
Temple  Church  in  London.           His  daughter  Eleanor  married  John
Steward  of  Axmouth.           His daughter  Jane  married at  Axmouth,     5
May,      1651,        Thomas Steward of Axmouth.       His son William Drake

Ezekiel  Hamlin of  Boston made his will 21 July,    1690.    In that

DUNN  (DONN)
THOMAS  DUNN had land granted to him in the "westerneck"
adjoining  on  the  south  the  land  of  Thomas  White.        (Weymouth
Land Grants,    270.)     Tho:   Donn,   aged 25,   came to New England in
the Defense in July,   1635.    (Hotten's  Original  Lists  of Emigrants,
1600-1700,      p.      106.)     He was made a freeman of  the  Massachusetts
Bay Colony,   26 May,    1647.    (Register,    3:   191.)     He married Mar-
garet      , who died at Weymouth,    10 May,   1659.    He drew a lot  at
Rehoboth,    30 June,    1644.    His share was forfeited,  24 Oct.  1643,    at
Rehoboth.               His name is  not on the register of lands  there in 1645.
He probably did not settle  in Rehoboth.       Savage says "he removed
to  Fairfield,    Conn.,   and there died in 1660,  without a wife or chil-
dren."
Thomas Donn had six  acres  in  the First  Division  and eighteen
acres  in  the  Second  Division  granted  to  him 14 Dec.  1663,      which
indicates  that he did not die in Fairfield,   Conn.,   in 1660,     as  Savage
asserted.                He was living  in Weymouth in  1679,    and then took the
oath of allegiance.
.
DYER
1.   DEA.          THOMAS  DYER was  born  undoubtedly  in  England
near 1612;     died at Weymouth,  6 or 15 Nov. 1676,   aged 63 or 64 years.
He married,    near 1640,   a woman traditionally reported to have been
named Agnes  Reed.          This  statement  appears  to  have  been made
about 1803 by Col. Asa White,   a descendant of the fifth generation.
It  is true that  Philip Reed of Weymouth,  in his will dated 15 Dec.
1674,       called  Thomas  Dyer  his  brother.       They  may have had one
mother,   or married sister,  or Reed may have married Dyer's sister,     or
Dyer may have married Reed's sister;   in any case they would call
each other brothers.         His first wife is  reported to have died at Wey-
mouth,     4 Dec.  1667.    He  married  (2)   Elizabeth  ( —)  Harding-
Frary,     widow successively  of Abraham Harding of Braintree and of
John Frary,     Jr.,   of Medfield.      She died before 3 Feb. 1679.
He settled in Weymouth before 1641,   and had seven acres granted
to him on King Oak Hill,    which had first  been granted to  Thomas
Holbrook.              He also  received  eleven acres  in  the First  Division  and
thirty- three acres in the Second Division,   14 Dec. 1663.    (Weymouth
Land Grants,     282,    283.)
 - 214 - 
210                                              DYER
He was  made a freeman of  the Massachusetts  Bay Colony,     29
May,   1644,    and on the same day was granted liberty "to  Keepe an
ordinary and sell wine at Waymoth. "    ( Massachusetts  Bay Colony
Records,     2:74.)    He served  as a deputy from Weymouth to the
General  Court  as  follows:    6  May,     1646;   26  May,     1647;   22  May,
1650;      18  May,    1653;    3  May,    1654;    14  May,     1656;    19  May,      1658;
30 May,    1660;    29 May,   1661;      27 May,    1663;    3 May,   1665;     23 May,
1666;     11 Sept.  1666;   29 Apr.  1668;    27 May,   1674;    7 Oct.  1674;    12
May,       1675 ;     9 July,    1675;  3 May,   1676 and 9 Aug.  1676.    He was
one of  three chosen by the General Court " to end small causes" at
Weymouth,   4 Nov. 1646,  "controvsyes under 20s.   for y yeere in Wei-
mouth. "    He was chosen a member of the committee " to determine
whether to erect a bridge at Naponsit River," 23 and 29 May,    1655.
The General  Court  granted him liberty  "to set  his tainters  in the
prison greene during the pleasure of this  Court, "  22 May,   1661.    He
was a "cloth-worker, "  and this undoubtedly referred to his  method
of advertising  his business in Boston.          He was a deacon of the First
Church of Weymouth from 1664  to  1676.    His  homestead was lo-
cated at Weymouth Heights on the old road leading  to  Hingham,
directly opposite the  Old North Church.
No evidence has been found that he had a twin son named Jonathan
Dyer,   born 10 July,    1643,  as published in the Vital Records of Wey-
mouth.             It is believed that Jno.  was interpreted as Jonathan.

1.   WILLIAM   DYER  ( Christopher,       William¹),     son  of  Christo-
pher  Dyer of Sheepscott,   Me. ,   and of Braintree,  with his wife Joanna
Chard  (daughter  of William  Chard,      born  at  Weymouth,      17  Aug.
1667),     was living  at Weymouth in 1693;     resided  in  Bridgewater,
1699 to  1708;      resided  in Weymouth 1712 to  1750.    He married (2)
(intention at  Weymouth,     17  Apr.  1712)   Mary Whitman,     daughter
of Abiah and Mary (Ford)   Whitman,     born at Weymouth,      14 Oct.
1683;   she died there 25 Sept. 1725.   She lived in John Pratt's house   568
at  Weymouth from  1704  to  1725,    which he gave her  by his  will
dated 12 July,    1714.    (Suffolk Probate Records,    19:     216.)     William
Dyer made his  will  10 Nov.  1749,    and it  was proved 15 Aug.  1750.
He bequeathed to  his  son  Christopher  Dyer land in Abington;        to
his daughter Jane,  widow of his son Joseph Dyer,   deceased,    his home-
stead  in  Weymouth;    to  his  granddaughters Sarah  Pratt  and Jane
Burrell;    to  the  children  of  his  son  Joseph,    deceased,    viz. ,     Joseph,
Benjamin,       Asa,      Stevens,      James,     Joanna  and  Mary  Dyer;       to  his
grandson  William  Dyer;     and to  the children of his daughter Eliza-
beth,     deceased.       (Suffolk  Probate,   44:    27-29. )
William Dyer of Weymouth, "being about 75 years old," deposed
31  Aug.  1738,     " that  he lived  with  his  grandfather  William  Dyer,
Esq. ,    near the old town of Sheepscott,    alias New Dartmouth,    county
of  Cornwall,       Me. ,     when there were two houses there wherein lived
with him the sd William Dyer,    Esq. ,   his second son John Dyer,    and his
only daughter Mary Bowles till  1689,   when his said grandfather and
his  father  Christopher  Dyer,     eldest  son,    were killed by the Indians,
his grandfather about 15 Aug. 1689,   and his father about Dec.  1689;
that he lived with his grandfather on Dyer's Neck about eleven
years.  "  etc.      (York County Deeds,    20:   225.)     Hence he was born
near  1653.    He returned to Weymouth near  1690.

ELLIS  (ALIE,    ELCE,    ELSE)
ROGER¹ ELLIS,  a weaver,   appeared at Yarmouth in 1641.    Plym-
outh  Colony Court granted him a license,   12 Nov. 1644,     to  marry
Jane  Lisham.           He removed to  Barnstable where he was living  in
1649,    and in June,  1654,   he was admitted an inhabitant  of Boston.
"Roger Alie & his wife Jane Alie" were admitted to the First Church
of  Charlestown,     "by a dismission  from  Waymoth  Ch. ",     20 Nov.
1659.    He died at  Charlestown,  (probably  Malden),   25 Dec.  1668.

FISHER
CORNELIUS  FISHER of Dedham lived in Weymouth in  1678-
79.    He was made a freeman  2  May,     1649,  and lived in  that  part
of  Dedham  which  became  Wrentham.            He probably  removed  to
Weymouth during  King  Philip's  War.           He married,    22 Feb.  1653,
Leah Heaton.        His children were born at Dedham,    including  his son
Cornelius,    who was born at Dedham,   8 Feb. 1659-60.         These were
among the Weymouth men who took the oath of allegiance in 1678-
79.   The Dedham and Wrentham Vital Records contain their families.

3.   SAMUEL  FORD (Andrew¹)  was born at Weymouth,   30 July,
1656;    died at  Weymouth,   6 Apr.  1711.    The record of his marriage
or the birth records of his children have not been preserved.             As the
three  sons  of Andrew Ford of  Weymouth-James,      Nathaniel  and
Samuel- were the heirs  of his  Connecticut land at "Quinnepoge, "
and as Nathaniel is  proved by a letter written in 1720-21  to be an
Uncle to John Ford of Hanover,   N. J.,   it is clear that Samuel Ford of
Weymouth was the father of John Ford of Hanover,     N. J.
Letter  from  Andrew Ford,    Jr.,    of Abington to  his  nephew John
Ford of Hanover,    N. J.:
" DEAR KINDSMAN:       I  am glad to hear of ye  welfare of weh  I have been apprized by
Mr.  Dean.            I  should be glad to see you but I  despair of it in this life  considering my
age and the distance of place of our habitations.      I and my wife are well (excepting the
infirmities  of old age).   My children also are well.        My son Hez.        is  lately  married
unto his second wife  (viz.)  unto  Sarah  Magoone our kindswoman and they
they arewell

FOSTER
JOHN  FOSTER was granted land that  had first  been  given  to
John Taylor,   and a second lot "upon the plaine" first given to William
Richards.            What became of him has not been ascertained.
THOMAS  FOSTER had  lands  granted  to  him  in  the  "East
ffield, "   first   given  to  John Allen  (Weymouth  Land Grants,       261.)
He certainly  resided  early  in  Weymouth,     1640.    He removed  to
Braintree  and to  Billerica before 1659.    He was made a freeman of
the Massachusetts Bay Colony,  26 May,  1647.   His wife was Eliza-
beth-.              For further  details  consult the  Thomas Foster  Record,
1889.
