FRENCH
1.   STEPHEN  FRENCH came probably  in  the ship  Mary and
John,     arriving  in  Boston Bay,    30 May,    1630.    He had a lot  of  16
acres  granted to him in Dorchester  towards " Naponsett, "  16 Jan.
1632-33,     and another of  8 acres granted 1  Dec.  1634.    (Dorchester
Town Records;      Register,     21 :    166,    276.)     He was made a  freeman
of the Massachusetts Bay Colony,   14 May,   1634.   He early removed
to  Wessagusset.         He had ten  acres  granted to  him  in  the  " East
field"  and fourteen acres in the "greate lotes" bounded on the east
with Hingham line.        (Weymouth Land Grants,     276.)     Lot No.  15
of 21 acres was granted to him in 1636.    He also had lots in the First
Division and in the Second Division granted to him,   14 Dec.  1663.
He was a Deputy from Weymouth,    12 Mar.  1637-38,    6 Sept.  1638,
and  15  Mar.  1638-39.            He also  was  appointed  a  Magistrate  for
Weymouth 6 Sept.  1638,    and a member of the Dorchester council in
Feb.  1638-39.            His wife was  Mary      , who died at  Weymouth,
6 Apr.  1655.    He died at Weymouth between 17  Mar. and 29 July,
1679.    His will is given briefly  in abstract.
Stephen French of Weymouth,  " being weake of body ",  made his
will as follows:      To the Church in Weymouth £4.          To his sister Mary
Randall  £3.                  Unto his  two grandsons  Stephen and Samuel his  land
in Hingham,     and land in Weymouth " neere Hockley, "  at 21 years.
To  his   three  granddaughters  Mary,      Hannah  and  Elizabeth   £10
apiece  at  18 years.           The residue  of  his  estate  he gave to  his  son
Stephen whom he appointed executor.            The deed lately made to his
Brother Searle of a part of the Spring lot in Weymouth he confirmed,
17  Mar.  1678-79.           William  Torrey and John  Whitman witnesses;
proved 29 July,   1679.    Further explanation of his will was made by
the testator,      18 Mar. 1678-79.        (Suffolk Probate Records,   6:   302.)
Children:
2.  Stephen,       b.     near 1640.
Josiah,     d.     at  Weymouth,   31 Jan.  1656-57.
2.   CAPT.          STEPHEN  FRENCH (Stephen¹)  was born in  Wey-
mouth near 1640;     died there 13 Mar. 1717-18.          He married at Wey-
mouth,      19 Sept.  1660,     Hannah Whitman,   daughter of John and Ruth
Whitman,     born at Weymouth,   24 Aug.  1641.    He was called Capt.
Stephen  French  in  1717.     He resided  on the  corner  of  East  and
Green streets,      North Weymouth.            He was made a freeman,       12 Oct.
1681.    (Register,   3:     246.)    He was deputy from Weymouth,    24 May,
1682.    How was he a brother to  Capt.    John Holbrook in  1699 ?     He
evidently married (2)  widow Hannah Loring.

during her natural life,    or  £12 a year if  she chooses to live elsewhere.

Stephen French of Weymouth,  yeoman,  being aged and indisposed
in body,    made his will following:       My personal estate to  be equally
divided  among  my eight  children,      viz. ,     Joshua,      Samuel,       David,
Jonathan,    Daniel,    Mercy and Hannah French and Elizabeth Blake.
To son Joshua French one-half of his dwelling house,    and west half
of his  barn,      and one-half of his land thereto  adjoining.     Also one-
half of a lot on the southeast side of the way to Hingham over against
his  son  Jonathan's  house  and  one-eighth  part  of his  corn  mill  in
Weymouth,       called  Bates's  Mill.         To  his  son  Samuel  French  the
other half of his house,    barn and one-half of his  land in Hockley
Field that was given him by his father-in-law Joshua Beal.            To his
son  David French land in the First Division in Abington on which
his  house and barn  standeth,    etc.     To  son Jonathan  French  land
near Pool's Cellar,   etc.;   also one-eighth of the sawmill in Weymouth

FRYE
GEORGE  FRYE was born near 1615,  "aged fifty Eight years  or
thereabouts,     heertofore of Comb St.  Nicholas.   [county  of Somerset]
in the Realme of England,   husbandman,   Living there untill the yeare
1640 in that yeare removed & came in the same shipp to New Eng-
land with William Torrey & Samuel  Torrey his sonn both of the sd
Comb St.  Nicholas & beeing arived in New England settled & ever
since have Lived in Weymouth, "  etc.    Deposed in Boston,     5 Mar.
1673-74.            (Suffolk Deeds,  8:    392.)    He was made a freeman of the
Massachusetts  Bay Colony,     7  May,    1651.    George  Frye  of Wey-
mouth,       weaver,   " being  subject  to  many distempers  bodily, "  made

daughter-in-law Mary Smith,   wife of James Smith,    Sr. ,    £5.               To his
daughter Ruth Torrey and to her son James Smith one-third of his
estate.            To his daughter Naomi Yeales,   one-third.          To his daughter
Bethiah   Reed,     one-third.          James  Smith,     Sr.   of  Weymouth  and
Timothy  Yeales  of  Boston,      executors.            Witnesses:      Alice  Howard,

two daughters Elizabeth and Mary.      His daughters to have two acres
of meadow and six  acres  "by the  mill"  and each  a "goate. "     To
Thomas Harris,    Thomas  Rawlens  and John Meigs,   his   three sisters'
youngest children ,    to  each a kid.         The rest  of his  estate  to his wife.
(Register,     2:     385.)     His  widow  Elizabeth  married  (2)  about  1643,

ZACCHEUS  GOULD appears  at  Weymouth as  early  as  1639.
On 28 Jan.  1639-40,    he was appointed overseer of the will of Henry
Russell  of  Weymouth.        James  Parker  of Strawberry  Bank  (Ports-
mouth,       N.  H.)  sells  Zaccheus Gould of  Ipswich  a house and nine
acres in Weymouth which he bought of Jeremy Gould 26 Nov. 1644,
and  Zaccheus  Gould of  Ipswich  sells  the  same  to  Capt.        William
Perkins,      2  Apr.  1645.    (Suffolk  Deeds,    1:56,    58.)    Jeremy Gould
sells  land  in  Weymouth to  Zaccheus Gould in  1639.    (Gould Gene-
alogy,     36.)      Zaccheus  Gould  came from  Hemel  Hempstead  and
King's  Langley,  county of  Herts,    to Weymouth near  1639,      and re-
moved to  Ipswich  and to  Topsfield  in  1644.    His wife  was Phebe
Deacon,   and their children were baptized at Hemel Hempstead,   viz.  ,
Phebe,   baptized 27 Sept.  1620,     Mary,    baptized  19 Dec.  1621,     and
Martha,       baptized  15 June,     1623.    His  daughter  Priscilla,     married
John  Wildes,     and  his  son John was  born 10 June,    1635,    probably
in  England.            (For  their  descendants  see  The Family  of  Zaccheus
Gould,     1895.)
GREEN
1.   JOSEPH  GREEN first  appears at  Plymouth in  a matter  of
arbitration,       2 Nov.  1640.    He held  12s.    1d.    in his  hands  in  a case
before  the  Plymouth  Colony  Court,    7  Dec.  1641,     and  was  named
among the Plymouth men able to bear arms in 1643.   He was named
to  go  on an expedition under Capt.    Myles Standish,    3 May,     1653.
John Morton of  Plymouth sells  Joseph Green of  Plymouth a house
there,     20 Feb.  1654,    and both  parties  consented  to  make the  deed
void.          (Mayflower Descendant,  9:  104.)   Joseph Green of Weymouth
made an  acknowledgment at  Plymouth relating  to  John  Saffin  of
Boston  concerning   his  carriage  in  Virginia,     29  Jan.  1657.     (Ibid.
12:80. )     It  is  not likely that the Weymouth man would have done
this at Plymouth had he not previously  lived in Plymouth.        Thirty
"about  Namassachesett  Ponds    were  granted  to  him  by
Plymouth  Colony,     2  Oct.   1660.     (Plymouth  Colony  Records,      3:
201.)     He was plaintiff  in a case before  Plymouth Colony Court of
Assistants,    5 Apr.  1692.
acres

GUPPY (GUPPEE)
JOHN  GUPPY of Weymouth was made a freeman of the Massa-
chusetts  Bay  Colony,    18  May,     1653.    (Massachusetts  Bay Colony
Records,     4:      Pt.     1,    p.    460.)    He received  seven acres  in  the  First
Division and twenty-one acres in the Second  Division,    14 Dec.  1663.
(Weymouth Land Grants,   282,   283.)     The estate of George Roapes
 - 255 - 
GURNEY                                251
ofSalem owedJohnGuppy £31s.  6d.   on 21 Dec. 1675.   (Essex County
Probate,   3:  36,   37.)
He was admitted as an inhabitant of Charlestown,   26 Feb.  1661-
62,      and was living  at George and Samuel Blanchard's there,  9 Aug.
1664.   He married Elizabeth         beforehe removed from Weymouth.
John Guppy and Elizabeth Guppy his  wife were admitted  to  the
First  Church  of  Charlestown,   4 July,    1680,     " By Dismission  from
ye  ch.     of Christ in Weymouth.  "    (Records of First Church of Charles-
town,      1632-1789,    p.     18.)
He buys of the heirs of Nathaniel Blanchard a house and lots  in
Weymouth  in  1686-87.              (Middlesex   County  Deeds,    10:76. )     He
deposed in  1678,    aged 60 years and his wife aged 72 years.           His wife
died at  Charlestown,    " an  aged woman,"  26 Aug.  1693.    He died
there 23 Feb.  1693-94.          They were probably somehow related to the
Weymouth families.      No children have been discovered in the early
records.
GURNEY
1.   JOHN  GURNEY,     Sr. ,   was born according  to  his  deposition,
made in  1653,   about 1603.    He was in Braintree before 1645.   Lands
were granted to him in Weymouth "in the East field," "in the mill
field"  and "on the east side of Great Pond" as early as 3 Feb.  1651-
52.     These lands were subsequently granted to others.        (Weymouth
Land Grants,     258,   270,    278,    282.)     Whether he ever resided in Wey-
mouth is a matter of doubt.       He owned land in Braintree,   which he
sold  12  Feb.  1661.    His  wife,     whose name is  apparently  unknown,
died at Braintree,   20 Sept.  1661.    He married (2) at Braintree,    12
Nov. 1661,   widow Grissell Kibbee,   successively the widow of Thomas
Jewell,        Henry Griggs,   and Henry Kibbee of Dorchester.         Her fifth

HARDING
JOHN¹ HARDING was made a freeman of the Massachusetts Bay
Colony,     13  May,     1640.    He early  settled  in  Weymouth.         He had
four acres granted to him in the "west field" which had been first
granted  to  Thomas  Holbrook and John  Whitmarsh.         He also  had
ten acres in the First Division and thirty acres in the Second Division
granted  him,      14  Dec.  1663.     (Weymouth  Land Grants,       263,      282,
283.)    He is  not named among the grantees of 1636.   Administration
on the estate  of John Harding,    late  of  Weymouth,    deceased,      was
granted to  John Whitmarsh in right  of his wife,    only  child  of said
Harding,      31  Oct.  1682.    The inventory was taken 2 Oct.  1682,     by
John  Holbrook,      Samuel  White  and  Stephen  French.             The  items
show  a  dwelling  house,    barn  and  land  adjoining  valued  at  £60,
several other  lots and twelve acres in " ragged plain. "    In the bond
John Whitmarsh was described as a " housewright. "    Babson in his
History of Gloucester,   page 97,   states that John Harding,   said to be
from Weymouth,   bought four acres in Gloucester of William Sargent
in  1652;   that  he married at  Gloucester  22 Apr.  1652,     the  Widow
Tybbot;    that  he was a selectman  of  Gloucester  in  1664,    sold  land
there to John Davis in 1665,   and disappears from the town.            Certainly
the Weymouth John Harding had lands granted to him at Weymouth
as  early as  1663,   and was owner of the same lands at the time of his
death shortly before 2 Oct.  1682.
Child:
Sarah,  2   m.     near 1654,   John Whitmarsh of Weymouth.
CAPT.       JAMES  HARDING was born near 1767,   married at Wey-
mouth,        22  July,      1790,       Mary  Ford,     daughter  of Capt.      James  and
Deborah  (Badlam)  Ford,    born at Weymouth,   6 Oct.  1771;    she died
at Weymouth,    15 Oct.  1839,   aged 67 or 68 years.       He died there 21
or  22 July,     1840,   aged 77 years.
He made his  will  23 Nov.  1838,      mentioning  his  sons  John  and
George  Harding,    if  living,    his  granddaughter  Antinel,     daughter  of
his  son Gideon Harding,  his wife,   Mary,   his  daughter Sally  S.,    wife
of Lewis Beals of Weymouth,   and his son Arthur Harding.        (Norfolk
Probate,     8770.)     The administrator states that sons John andGeorge
have not  been  heard  from,    one  for  about  twenty-four  years,     and
the other for about ten years.

HARRIS
WALTER HARRIS earliest appears in a list of sixteen men,  "such
men as  are  to  be transported to New England to be resident  there
uppon a plantacon, " 7 Mar.  1631.     (Hotten's Original Lists  of Emi-
grants,        1600-1700,     p.     149.)     He was made a freeman of the Massa-
chusetts  Bay Colony,  2 June,    1641.    It  is  stated in the Pioneers  of
Massachusetts that he came to Plymouth upon an engagement with
Mr. John Atwood of London,   was under the command of Mr. John
Doane  of  Plymouth for  five  years,   but  was transferred  to  Henry
Howland,    8 Apr. 1633.    Granted these facts to be true,   then he set-
tled  in  Weymouth near  1637.    He married  Mary Frye,      sister   to
William  Frye of Weymouth,    who bequeathed to  Thomas Harris,    to
Hannah,     the wife of Thomas Rawlins of Weymouth,   and to  Tama-
zine,      the wife of John Meigs of Weymouth,    and of Guilford,     Conn.  ,
his three sisters'   youngest children.        She died at New London,    Conn. ,
24 Jan.  1656.    (New England Historical and Genealogical Register,
2:  385.)
Walter Harris had lands granted to him in the "west ffield,  "  first
given to  Robert  Lovell,   and eight  acres  in  "Harrises  Raing"  and
 - 260 - 
256                                                HART
eight acres in the "mill furlonge" in Weymouth.       (Weymouth Land
Grants,     255.)      He also  had lot  No. 12 of the great lots on the east
side  of Fresh Pond,  recorded 26 Nov. 1651.    He was one of the ap-
praisers of the estate of John Pope of Dorchester,   1 June,   1649.    He
removed from Weymouth to  Dorchester near 1649.    The New Lon-
don,     Conn. ,     town records  show under date of 20 May,      1652,      that
Walter Harris of Dorchester "desires a house lot," which was granted.
He was licenced as "an ordinary keeper" there 6 June,   1654,   and died
there,     6 Nov.  1654.    His widow made her will at New London,    19
Jan.  1655,     showing her connection with the Frye,    Meigs and Raw-
lins  families  of Weymouth,   which see in Caulkins's History of New
London,   Conn. ,   page 270.
Children:

HART
EDMUND HART probably came in the Mary andJohn,     arriving
at  Dorchester  in  1630,    having landed at Nantasket,   30 May,     1630.
Thecompany settled in Dorchester on or about 17 June, 1630,  and Mr.
Hart was granted land there in 1632.    He was made a freeman of the
Massachusetts  Bay  Colony,     14  May,    1635.    The town records  of
Dorchester  show that  Edmond Hart et  al.   "are to  have their  great
lotts  of 16 acres a peece,    next the great lotts that are all redy layde
owt towardes  Naponsett,"  16 Jan.  1632.    (Register,    21 :    166.)     He
had 18 acres  granted to him in Weymouth in 1636,   and 11 acres  in
the "East field" and 3 acres at "Kingoke hill. "     He also had 7 acres
in the First Division and 21 acres in the Second Division granted to
him,   14 Dec. 1663.    (Weymouth Land Grants,   261,   280,   283. )   Savage
conjectures that he removed from Weymouth to Westfield after 1664,
and that he was the man there killed by lightning in 1673.    His wife
died at Weymouth,    20 Aug.  1659.
Children:
Elisha,     d.     1683.
Sarah,      m.      near  1675,    John Scoon (Scone)  of  Westfield,    and lived
there  1676-83.
Martha,    b.    at Weymouth,    12 Oct.  1640;   m.   24 Jan.  1662,     Edward
Neale of Weymouth and Westfield.
-,  m.     John Greet of Westfield.

1.   JOHN   HAWES (John,      John,3  John,       Edward ¹)  was  born at
Sharon,      24 Dec.  1748,    and baptized there 15 Jan.  1748-49;     died at
Weymouth,     9 or 10 Mar. 1836,   aged 90 years.          Mr.  Frank Mortimer
Hawes of Somerville has made an exhaustive study of the descendants
of Richard  Hawes and of Edward Hawes,    and he believes  that John
Hawes of Weymouth was the son of John and Amy (Morgan)  Hawes
of Sharon and of  Boston.             About 1755 they removed to Boston,    and
the father apparently died between 2 Apr.  1756,   and Dec.  1757,    and
Amma Hawes,   probably his widow,   married in Boston,  10 Dec. 1757,
John  Williamson.              The father  and  the  grandfather  each  had  sons
named John,       Joseph  and  Samuel.            The  Columbian  Centinel,      pub-
lished  in  Boston,     12  Mar.  1836,     under  deaths,     reports,      " In  Wey-
mouth,       Mr. John Hawes,   aged 90. "

HEWES  (HUGHES)
WILLIAM  HEWES was an abutter to  the land granted  to  Rev.
Samuel  Newman by the town of  Weymouth.           (Land Grants,      260.)
That this  man had land  granted  to him by the  town before  Rev.
Samuel Newman removed to Rehoboth in 1643 or 1644,    there cannot
be the shadow of a doubt.         His surname was perhaps Hughes.
A William  Hewes or  Hughes was at  New Medow (Topsfield)   at
the farm where he now lives,    13 Aug.  1643.    In July,    1644,    he and
his  son John Hewes were  presented  at  the  Salem  Quarterly  Court
" for  deriding  such  as  sing  in  the  congregation "  and  for  remarks
against  Mr.  Whiting.        In Apr.  1648,    he was haled into court for not
contributing  to  the  maintenance of  the  minister.          Purnell  Hughes,
wife  of William Hughes of  Lynn,     acknowledged that  she had been
"selling strong waters without license whereby one was distempered,  "
16 Oct.  1650.     ( Massachusetts Bay Records,  4,   Pt.    1:     31.)
HICKS
•   JOHN  HICKS came from London to  Weymouth near 1636.    He
had a grant of land which was later granted to James Nash.           (Wey-
mouth Land Grants,   276.)    He married in St.  Faith's parish,    London,
near  1636,         Herodias  or  Horod  Long.              They lived  in  Weymouth
about two and one-half years.        They removed  to  Newport,     R.  I. ,
in  1639.    Shortly  thereafter  Hicks  obtained  the  most of his  wife's
property and deserted her,    removing to  Newtown,      L.  I. ,     as  early  as
1656,      when he was there  taxed  £1  10s.            (Riker's  Annals  of New-
town,         43.)      He later  removed  to  Hempstead,       L.  I.      His  deserted
wife Herodias  married  (2)   George Gardiner  of Newport and became
a Quakeress.              She revisited Weymouth in 1658 and was whipped and
imprisoned for her faith.
On 11  May,        1658,       Horod Gardiner  "being  the mother of many
children,       came with  her babe at  her  brest  from  Newport  to  Wey-
mouth,      to deliver  her religious testimony,   for which she was carried
to  Boston,      before  Gov.  John  Endicott,     who  sentenced  her  to  be
whipped with ten lashes,     as  well  as  her companion  Mary Stanton,
who came with her to help bear her child.       After the whipping with
a three- fold  knotted  whip of cords,     she  was continued for  fourteen
days longer in prison.  "
Bishop's  New England Judged says:     " The  woman came a very
sore journey,     and (according to man)   hardly accomplishable,   through
a wilderness of above sixty miles,   between Rhode Island and Boston. "
(Austin's Genealogical Dictionary of Rhode Island,    81.)
 - 271 - 
HILLARD -HOLBROOK                         267
"The petition of Horod Long alias Gardiner, wife of George Gardiner
of Newport,     dated 3 May,   1665,   declares that when her father died
in England she was sent to London and was there married,   unknown
to her friends,   to John Hicks,  privately in the under church of Paul's
called  St.  Faith's  Church,    she being between thirteen  and fourteen
years  old.                She then came to  New England with her  husband and
lived  at  Weymouth two and a half years,     thence  coming  to  Rhode
Island about the year 1640,   and there lived ever since,     till  she  came
to Pettacomscott.       Soon after coming to Rhode Island there happened
a difference between her and her husband John Hicks,  and he went
away to the Dutch,   carrying with him most of her estate,   which had
been sent  her  by her  mother.         (Her  mother  and  her  brother  lost
their  lives  and estate  in his  Majesty's  service,     she  says. )    After her
desertion  by John Hicks  she  became the  wife  of  George Gardiner,
and by him had many children.
"As to the marriage of George Gardiner,    Robert Stanton testified
that one night at his house both of them did say,  before him and his
wife,     that  they did take one the other,    as  man and wife.
"Horod Gardiner,    having lived with her last  husband eighteen  or
twenty years,      now desired of the Assembly that the estate and labor
he [Gardiner]   had of mine,  may be allowed to me and the house upon
my land  I  may enjoy  without  molestation  and that  he may allow
me my child to bring up,   with maintenance for her,    and that he be
restrained  from troubling  me more.  "
She,      the  mother  of  sixteen  children,    married  (3)  John  Porter  of
Kingston,     R.  I.

HOLBROOK
1.   THOMAS  HOLBROOK,  his  wife Jane,   their sons John,    aged
11 years,     Thomas,  aged 10 years,   and daughters,   Anne,   aged 5 years,
and Elizabeth,   aged 1 year,     sailed  from Weymouth on or near 20
Mar.  1634-35  with  Rev. Joseph  Hull's  Company.        He came from
Broadway,        Somersetshire,      Eng.
Thomas Holbrook,   aged 77 years or thereabouts,  deposed that he
came to New England with Mr. Hull's Company in  1635,     and that
they  came ashore at  Dorchester,   7 June,    1635;  that  they  went  to
Dorchester and the Company went to a place now called Weymouth;
and that after remaining at Dorchester about a fortnight,     he went
with his family to the now Weymouth,   and built a house there,   etc. ,
sworn to in court,  2 Nov. 1666.    (Suffolk Court Files,    815.)
It is apparent that he was born near 1589 and that he was married
to  Jane -,                     perhaps Kingman -near  1617.    He died at Wey-
mouth shortly before 10 Mar.  1677.    There is  a statement that  his
wife was Jane Kingman,   born near  1600,   but no authentic record of
this fact,    has been found by the compiler.
 - 272 - 
268                                          HOLBROOK
He was made a freeman of Massachusetts Bay Colony,   May,    1645;
townsman (selectman),  1645,   1646,   1651,   1652,   and 1654.    Ten acres
were granted  to him in the  First  Division and thirty  acres  in  the
Second  Division,     14  Dec.  1663.    (Weymouth  Land  Grants,         283,
284.)
"Being sick and weak"  he made his will 31 Dec. 1668,   bequeathing
unto his wife Jane,  his sons John Holbrooke,     William  Holbrook and
Thomas Holbrook,    and unto his daughters Anne Rennolds,   Elizabeth
Hatch,     and Jane Drake and unto his  grandchildren John  Holbrook,
Peter Holbrook and William Holbrook,  and to all of his grandchildren
that shall be living at his wife Jane's death,   his property.         He stated
that his grandson Peter Holbrook had served him and his wife in their
old age for about eight years,  for which he was to have his dwelling
house in Weymouth with the orchard and arable land.           This will he
confirmed 31 Dec. 1673,  and it was proved 24 Apr. 1677.    His inven-
tory,     taken 10 Mar. 1677,    calls  him "late of Weymouth dec'd.  "

HOLLARD
ANGELL  HOLLARD,   aged 21,   his wife Katherine,   aged 22,     their
servant  George Land,   aged  22,   and the latter's  kinswoman Sarah
Land,      aged  18,    sailed  from  Weymouth  in  Dorsetshire  with  Rev.
Joseph  Hull's  Company,    on or  near  20  Mar.  1634-35,     and arrived
at  Dorchester 7 June,    1635.    He was the son of Hugh Hollard  of
Netherbury,     county of Dorset,   and the grandson of Thomas Hollard
of  Waytowne in  the  same  county.        (Register,    64:   346-347.)     He
married at Beaminster,    county of Dorset,    12 Aug. 1634,      Katherine
Richards,   born near  1612.    He was baptized at Netherbury,    10 Apr.
1614.    His  father  was buried in that parish,  26 Aug. 1655.    (Ibid.
64: 347;    68:61.)
Angell Hollard  was  made a freeman  of  the  Massachusetts  Bay
Colony,    3 Mar.  1635-36.             He early settled in Weymouth and had
two lots granted to him in " the east  field," the second having first
been granted to the Widow Streame.          He was a shoemaker and re-
moved to Boston where " his  house now a building"  was located on
the north side of Joseph Phippeny,   8 Sept. 1647.   (Register,    63 :    382.)
Apparently his six eldest children were born in Weymouth,    although
their  births  were  recorded  in Boston.            The baptisms  of his  fifth,
sixth  and  seventh child at the First Church of Boston describe him
as  a " member of the Church of Weymouth,"  1644 to 1649.    In the
Register  (63 :    382)   the  contributor  supposes  that  he  returned  to
England in  1654.    If so,    he returned  to  Boston and died there 30
June,    1670.    His widow Catherine Hollard presented his  inventory
to  the  Probate Court 26 July,    1671.    It  shows that she  paid "ye
passage of  his  widdow and daught   hither  £12 "  and sent a bill  of
exchange  " to   Mr.  Thomas  Hollard  in  England  to  whom Angell
Hollard owes about  £150.  "      (Ibid.     63:    383.)    His  widow contracted
marriage,      14 Aug. 1671,  with John Upham,   Sr.,    of Malden,   and was
called Catherine Upham in June,     1672.
Children,    first  six born in Weymouth but recorded in Boston:
Hannah, 2  b.    8 Oct. 1635;     m.   (1)  23 July,    1652,    William Ballantine
of Boston,     and m.    (2)   William Long.
Elizabeth,       b.       7 July,   1638;      m.      (1)   John  Brooking,    and m.      (2)
Edward Grove.
Thomas,    b.     7 May,   1641;   d.    young.
Hepzibah,     b.      10 Aug. 1642.
Thomas,     b.       8 Oct.  1644;    bp.   10 Nov. 1644,    ae.    about 5 wks.
Sarah,    b.     5 Mar. 1646-47;   bp.    7 Mar. 1646-47 ae.   about 4ds.
John,     bp.    27 May,   1649,   ae.    about 6 ds.
Mary,   bp.    14 Sept.  1651.
Joanna,    b.      17 Dec.  1653;   d.    29 Mar.  1654.

HOLLIS
1.   JOHN  HOLLIS  was  born  near  1645,    probably  in  England;
died at Weymouth between 12 Dec.  1700,    and 9 Jan.  1700-01.               He
married as  early  as  1663,     Elizabeth  Priest,  daughter of James  and
Elizabeth  Priest  of Weymouth.          She survived  her husband and ad-
ministered upon his estate,  9 Jan.  1700-01  (his son Samuel,    the other
executor,      being a minor).          He was one of the Weymouth men who
served in King Philip's  War.       He was in Capt.     Isaac Johnson's Com-
pany at  Dedham,   10 Dec.  1675,   and was credited  £4 10s.    10d.         for
services  under Capt.   Jonathan Remington,   24 June,   1676.    His son
Samuel Hollis was one of the grantees of Narraganset Township No.
5 (Bedford and parts of Merrimac and Manchester,    N.  H.)   in right
of his  father John Hollis  of Weymouth in  1733.    (Bodge's  Soldiers
in  King Philip's  War,    162,    279,     433.)
John Hollis,    Sr. ,    of Weymouth,  being weak of body,   made his will
12 Dec.  1700,     and it  was proved 9 Jan.  1700-01.               To his  son  John
Hollis  he  gave  10s.             To his  son Samuel  Hollis   all   his  lands  and
housing in  Weymouth after the decease of his wife Elizabeth Hollis.
To his daughter Elizabeth Hollis 5s.          To his daughter Hannah Hollis
his movables.           His wife to have all his estate during her natural life.
His wife and son Samuel to be executors.         His loving friends  John
Burrell   and  Joseph  Green  to   be  overseers.                   Witnesses:           Joseph
Green,       John  Burrell  and  Zachariah  Gurney,     his   mark.              (Suffolk
Probate Records,    14:  273.)
Children,   born at Weymouth:
John, 2  b.    28 Mar. 1664;     m.    Mary  - and had,     at Weymouth,
John,          b.       26  Nov.  1691.     He removed  to  Braintree  about
1694 and settled  there.       He is the ancestor  of  the Braintree
Hollises.
Thomas,    b.      7 Jan.  1666-67;      not mentioned in his father's  will ;
probably d.      young.
Elizabeth,     b.        18  Nov.  1669;      unm.    12 Dec.  1700.
Hannah,     unm.     12 Dec.  1700.
Mercy,     b.     5 Feb.  1674-75;    not mentioned in her father's  will,
12  Dec.  1700;   probably d.   young.
2.  Samuel,     under age 9 Jan.  1700-01 .

HOLLISTER
JOHN  HOLLISTER was  made a freeman of  the  Massachusetts
Bay Colony,   10 May,   1643.    He settled in Weymouth and had land
in the "west ffield," which had first  been granted to  William  How-
land,   granted to him.        He was a deputy from Weymouth to the Gen-
eral  Court,     7  Mar.  1643-44.           He was a "Townsman"  (selectman)   of
Weymouth in 1645 and 1646,   and perhaps in 1648.    Apparently he
did not long  remain at Weymouth but returned to England.             John
Hollister of the precincts of the castle in the city of Bristol,    Glouces-
tershire,      cordwainer,    being aged,   made his will 12 Sept.  1690,    and it
was proved 5  Dec.  1690.    He gave to his  cousin Samuel Hollister  of
Burrington,      Somerset,    the  management of the ground  there  in  the
parish of Huntspil,   Somerset,   called Catchams,   and the ground called
Torreys,        wherein  Capt.        William  Torrey  and  his  son  Mr.  Samuel
Torrey hath lease for their lives in it,    both living in New England,   he
 - 302 - 
298                                            HOVEY
to collect rents till otherwise ordered by them in NewEngland.       (Reg-
ister,   40:    62.)     His association  in Bristol,  Eng.,  with the Torreys  of
Weymouth must  be  considered as  identifying  evidence  connecting
John Hollister  of Weymouth in 1643 with John Hollister  of Bristol,
"aged,"  in  1690.    He must be distinguished from John Hollister  of
Wethersfield,    Conn.         (Hollister Family,  30,    31.)

brother Joseph Benson of Hull,   cordwainer,  all rights in the estate of
her father who had deceased,  in Hull,  2 Jan. 1706.    She died at Wey-
mouth 26 Mar. 1735.    He married (2)  at Weymouth,  13 Νοv.   1735,
widow Sarah King of Norton.
He was a blacksmith and lived in the South Parish 1703 to  1756.
He sold for  £90 to  Nathaniel  Searle of Weymouth 25 acres  there,     5
June,     1710,      and 50 acres  in the "Pond plain, "  on the south  side  of
Pond River,     to Thomas Hunt of Weymouth,   18 Apr. 1739.     (Suffolk
Deeds,       25 :     150;   60:    199.)      He made his will 9 July,   1744,    and it  was

HOWE
DR.      APPLETON HOWE,  son of Rev. Nathaniel and Olive (Jones)
Howe,    was born at  Hopkinton 26 Nov. 1792;   died at Weymouth,    10
Oct.  1870.    He graduated from Harvard College in  1815,     and from
the Harvard Medical School in 1819;    physician at South Weymouth,
1819 to 1870;  member and commander of the Ancient and Honorable
Artillery  Company;    surgeon,    adjutant,   colonel,   brigadier and major-
general of Massachusetts Volunteer Militia;   state senator 1841,    1842
and 1843.    He married (1) at Weymouth,  12 Dec. 1821,   Harriet Loud,
daughter  of Eliphalet  and Anna (Blanchard)   Loud,     born at Wey-
mouth,    8 Feb. 1795,   and died there 16 Nov. 1848,    in her 54th year.
He married  (2),    about  1850,     Eliza  Loud,   daughter  of  Joseph  and

REV.     JOSEPH HULL,  son of Thomas and Joan (Peson)  Hull,   was
born at  Crewkerne,     Somersetshire,     near  1595;  died at  the  Isle  of
Shoals,       N.  H.,    19  Nov. 1665.    Thomas Hull and Johane Peson were
married  in  the  parish  of  Crewkerne,      11  Jan.  1572-73.           (Somerset
Parish  Registers,   5:   6.)    At the age of 17 years
ears  he matriculated at
St.  Mary's Hall,   Oxford University,   22 May,   1612,   and was admitted
to  the degree B.A.  14 Nov.  1614.    His matriculation calls  him "son
of  a  commoner. "    He was instituted  rector  of  Northleigh  (North
Leigh)  in the county of Devon,   4 Apr.  1621,    on the presentation of
Thomas Hull of Crewkerne,    Somerset.         He resigned there  in  1632.
In the vicinity of Crewkerne he gathered a company of 106 souls,  who,
under his  leadership,    sailed from Weymouth in Dorset on or near 20
Mar.  1634-35.         They landed at Dorchester on 7 June,  1635  (Thomas
Holbrook's  deposition),  "and  Mr.  Hull  and Company went to  the
place that is  now called Weymouth. "    He was made a freeman of
the  Massachusetts  Bay Colony,   2  Sept.  1635.    Under  the  date  8
July,     1635,     John Winthrop  wrote:  "At this  court Wessaguscus was
made a plantation and Mr. Hull,   a minister of England,   and twenty-
one families with him allowed to sit  down there.  "
He was an Episcopal  clergyman,    and soon removed  to  Hingham
where a house lot was granted to him on the "Lower Plain.  "     He was
adeputy from Hingham to the General Court, 7 Sept. 1638,   and again,
13 Mar. 1638-39.
He received a grant  of land at Weymouth,   12 June,   1636.    His
son Benjamin was baptized at Hingham,  24 Mar. 1639.    In his diary
Rev. Peter Hobart,   minister at Hingham,   wrote,   under date of 5 May,
1639,       that  Mr.  Hull  preached his  farewell  sermon,     either  at  Wey-
mouth or at Hingham,          He removed to Barnstable and was made a
freeman of  the  Plymouth  Colony,    3  Dec.  1639.    He was at  Yar-
mouth in 1641 and at Barnstable in 1642 and 1643.    He then removed
to York,    Me.  ,   where he was recorded as minister 10 May,   1643.    He
returned to England in  1652 and was rector  of St.  Buryan in Corn-
wall.         He returned to New England,   where his family had remained
since 1635,       and was the minister  at  Oyster  River  (now Durham) ,
N.  H.    He was not in favor with the magistrates  of either  Massa-
chusetts Bay or  Plymouth Colony.          His first  wife's  name is  appar-
entlyunknown.    He married (2), before 20 Mar. 1634-35 Agnes -,
the mother of his seven youngest children.

'HUMBER
EDWARD  HUMBER was admitted to the First Church of Salem
from the First  Church of Weymouth,   5 June,   1664.    (Essex  Insti-
tute  Collections,    15:   77.)    He was made a freeman of the Massa-
chusetts  Bay Colony  at  Salem,    3 May,    1665.    (Register,      3 :     239) ;
Juror at  Salem,    28 Nov.  1665;  constable there 6 July,    1667.    His
wife was not here,   but he had sent for her before 26 Jan.  1668.    He
rented a smith's shop in 1671,  showing that he was a blacksmith.

2.   DEA.      JONAS  HUMPHREY,    Jr.  (Jonas¹) ,  was born probably
at Wendover,     near  1620;    died at Weymouth,    9 or 11 Feb.  1698-99,
aged 79 years.         He married near  1648,    Martha     , the mother of
his  children.                He removed from Dorchester to Weymouth near  1653
and had seven  acres  in  the  First  Division  and twenty acres  in the
Second Division granted to him,  14 Dec. 1663.    He was a deacon of
the First Church and resided on Neck Street in " Old Spain. "
Jonas  Humphrey,  aged 68 years  or  thereabouts,   deposed that he
lived  for  some time  in  Wendover,    county  of  Bucks,    and was well
acquainted with Enoch Hunt of Titenden,  parish of Lee,    about two
miles  distant  from Wendover,    blacksmith,    and with Ephraim Hunt,
blacksmith,     reputed eldest  son of said  Enoch  Hunt,   and that  they
afterwards  removed into  New England and for  some time dwelt at
Weymouth,    and that said  Enoch Hunt,    the father,    soon returned to
England,    but his  son Ephraim Hunt remained at Weymouth,     there
married,    had several  sons,   and continued his  dwelling  there  to the
time of his  death,     about  sixteen  months  since,     etc.,     2  July,       1688.
(Massachusetts Archives,   129:    16.)

HUNT
1.   ENOCH  HUNT came from the parish of Lee in Buckingham-
shire Eng.  ,    to Weymouth.           He received 22 acres "in the plaine" and
one acre near  "burying Iland. "     On 2July,  1688,    " Jonas Humphrey
and Robert Randall,   both of Weymouth,  deposed that they lived in
Wendover for  some time,   and that they were acquainted with Enoch
Hunt of Titenden,   in the parish of Lee,   about two miles distant from
Wendover,     blacksmith,    and his eldest  son Ephraim  Hunt,    and that
the said Enoch and his son Ephraim afterwards removed into  New
England and for some time dwelt in Weymouth,    and that the said
Enoch Hunt,    the father,  soon returned again to England,   but his son
Ephraim remained and settled in Weymouth,   and there married and
had issue several sons,  and continued to dwell there  to  the time  of
his  death,      about  sixteen  months  since."    ( Massachusetts Archives,
129:   16.)
He probably came as early as 1639 and died in England some time
before  1647.    He married  in  England,      near  1609,     a woman who
probably died before he came to New England.        He married perhaps
at Dorchester,     near 1639,   widow Dorothy Barker,    who survived him,
and married (3)  John King of Weymouth.        Her will was dated 14
June andproved 21 Oct.  1652.
Administration on his estate,   not yet administered,   was granted to
his son Ephraim Hunt,   18 Nov. 1652.
Children by first wife,  born in England:
2.  Ephraim,       b.    near 1610.
Peter,    m.    at Rehoboth,  14 Dec. 1646,   Elizabeth Smith.           He was
one  of  the  first   purchasers  of  Rehoboth  about  1643,    his
allotment being valued at £327.
Childby wife Dorothy,  born at Weymouth:
Sarah,      b.      4 July,   1640;  m.     1  Aug.  1661,     Matthew Pratt,     2d,
ofWeymouth.

JACKSON
EDMUND¹ JACKSON with his wife Mary -      resided  in Brain-
tree,      Weymouth and Abington from  1691  to  1724.    He was of the
right  age  to  have been the youngest son of Edmund and his  third
wife  Elizabeth  (Pilkington)   Jackson,    who was  born  in  Boston,       2
Aug.  1672.    That child's father died in Boston before 2 May,     1675,
and his widow married  (2)  at  Marblehead,    16 Dec.  1676,      William
Beale,     Sr. ,     of  Marblehead.          Edmund Jackson,    Sr.,    of Boston,     1635 to
1675,     had a large family,   including  a son Samuel born in Boston,    27
June,     1643.     On 22 Feb.  1695-96,    Samuel Jackson of Boston,     cord-
wainer,      " only  son  and heir  apparent  of  Edmond Jackson,     late  of
Boston,      cordwainer, "   sells   Joshua  Gee  of  Boston,      shipwright,       all

rights in the estate of his father as one of the Proprietors of Boston.
(Suffolk Deeds,    17:     270.)   As our Edmund Jackson was living at the
time the aforesaid  deed was executed,    he could not be a brother  of
Samuel  Jackson  of  Boston who styled  himself the  only  son  of Ed-
mund Jackson of Boston,    1635 to  1675.    Our Edmund Jackson left
no  recorded  deeds  in  Suffolk  County.       Two  of  his  children  were
recorded as born in Weymouth,    one was recorded as born in Braintree,
and all  were recorded as  born in Abington.            The probability is  that
he resided  near  Braintree line  in  1696,    and at  other  times near  the
line  between  Weymouth and Abington.        He died  at  Abington,      26
Feb.  1723-24.         His widow Mary died there 5 July,  1737.

JEFFREY  (JEOFFERIES)
ROBERT  JEFFREY,   aged "30 yeres,"  Marie his  wife,    aged 27,
and three children,    Thomas,  aged 7,   Elizabeth 6,   and Mary 3,     came
to New England in the ship Elizabeth and Ann,  Roger Cooper,   mas-
ter,        in  May,        1635.    (Hotten's  Original  Lists  of  Emigrants,       77.)
 - 338 - 
334                                          JEFFRIES
Samuel Butterworth deposed 2 Nov. 1666 "yt ye home lott yt was
first  given to Robert Jefferyes in Waymouth about 31 years since was
six acres more or lesse & lying  in  Waymouth aforesd  nere a place
there called King oake hill. "    (Suffolk Court Files,   815,   14th paper.)
He again deposed that he bought of Jeffery "a little  house and land
at Waymoth"  for himself and his brother and sister,   and that they
enjoyed it  for about nine or ten years,  26 July, 1665,  stating that this
occurred about 34 years  since.       Hence it  was approximately  1635.
In the deposition of Thomas Holbrook,    Sr.,    2 Nov.  1666,   he testified
that the home lot was given to Jeffery "in Weymouth about one and
thirty  years, "  which would tend to  fix  the date in  1635.    He also
stated that  Robert Jefferys  stayed there "but a little while doubtles
not three monthes. "    However,  at a Meeting,  2Feb. 1651-52,   Robert
Jeffery had a share in the great lots on the east side of "Fresh Pond. "
It was the attempt to sell these lands without settling upon them and
occupying them for a period of years that led the town to question
the rights of several persons so to do.           He removed to Rhode Island
in 1638 and was at Newport in 1646.
JEFFRIES
WILLIAM  JEFFRIES,  a gentleman,  came to Wessagusset with the
Gorges Company in Sept.  1623,   and was one of the principal inhabi-
tants of that place in 1628.    On 21 Apr. 1629,   William Jeffryes,    gen-
tleman,   and William Blackstone,   clericus,   were authorized to put John
Oldham in possession of certain lands granted to him on the banks of
the Charles River.
On 1 Apr. 1626,  he had a legacy bequeathed by his mother,    of two
houses and a bake house and ale house with the sign of Cordelyon,
anciently known as Flower de Luce; in Southwark,   Eng.
He made application for admission to  Massachusetts Bay Colony
as a freeman 19 Oct. 1630,  and took the freeman's oath 18 May,   1631.
Hereceived a remembrance of ten shillings for a ring from his brother-
in-law Hugh Evans of  London in 1636.
The letter which Governor Bradford sent to his Majesty's Council
for New England,  dated 9 June,  1628,  sets forth that "some of the
chief of every plantation" had subscribed towards the charge of send-
ing back to England Mr. Thomas Morton,   as follows :
From Plymouth                                                                                              £2:    10
From Naumkeak [Salem]                                                                                                                                                                     1:10
From Pascataquack [Little  Harbor,    N. H.]                                                                                                                 2:10
From Mr. Jeffrey and Mr. Burslem [Wessagusset]                                                                                                        2: 0
From Natascot [Hull]                                                                                                                                                              1:10
From Mrs. Thompson [Thompson's Island,  Boston Harbor]                                                                           : 15
From Mr.  Blackston [Boston]                                                                                                                              : 12
From Edward Hilton [Dover Point]                                                                                                                                                                             1: 0
(Collections of Mass.    Hist.     Soc. ,    First  Sec. ,   3:  63.)
He was one of the chief of the plantation who contributed to the
expense of sending  Thomas Morton back to England before 9 June,
 - 339 - 
JENNER                                  335
1628.    (See Bursley.)    He was deputed by John Gorges,    son of Sir
Ferdinando Gorges,    as one of his agents to put Mr. John Oldham in
possession  of  his  grant,    on 21 Apr.  1629.    (Suffolk  County Deeds,
1:       xiii .)     There is  no documentary evidence showing that he resided
at  Salem,      at Jeffreys  Creek,    at the  Isles  of Shoals or  in  Boston,    al-
though he may have had business relations with the old planters in
thoseplaces.
He was called "my very good gossip"  by Thomas Morton from
whom he carried  a letter  to  Governor  Winthrop  on 4 Aug.  1634.
(Savage's  edition of  Winthrop's History  of New England,     1630-49,
Vol.       1 :     164.)     Winthrop then called Jeffrey "an old planter. "    He
was a sergeant in the Pequot War in 1637,   and was commissioned by
the General Court for Weymouth "to see people joyne in marriage,    &
Keepe record thereof" on 2 June,   1641.    (Massachusetts Bay Colony
Records  1:    329.)     He married,   near  1640,  Mary Gould,   daughter of
Jeremiah and Priscilla  (Grover)  Gould of  Weymouth.       He was one
of the witnesses  to  the  Indian deed of land  in the town,   26 April,
1642.    (Nash's  History  of  Weymouth,    252.)     With  his  family  he
removed to  Newport,   R. I.,   about 1650.    Five children.            (See Aus-
tin's  Genealogical Dictionary of Rhode Island,     111.)
Child,  born at Weymouth:
Mary, 2  b.    20 Mar.  1642.
JENNER
1.   THOMAS  JENNER,    a  farmer,     as  is  learned  from  his  son's
matriculation record,    was living at Fordham,   county of Essex,     Eng-
land,     in 1623,    and emigrated to New England about 1635.    He first
settled  at  Roxbury,    and in  1636 removed to  Weymouth.           He had
there a grant of 18 acres as Mr. Jenner,   Sr.,   and at the same time Mr.
Jenner,    Jr.,      had 45 acres granted to him.      He was made a freeman
of the Massachusetts  Bay Colony,    8 Dec.  1636.    He was a deputy
to  the Great and General  Court  from  Weymouth,    13  May,      1640.
He apparently died before 28 Dec.  1649.
Child,  born at Fordham,   county of Essex:
2.  Thomas,      Jr.,2  b.    near 1605.
2.   REV.       THOMAS  JENNER (Thomas¹)  was born at  Fordham,
county of Essex,   England,    near 1605;  died in England in 1686 (Reg-
ister,       46:     174.)     He  matriculated  as  a  sizar  at  Christ's   College,
University of Cambridge,  16 Feb. 1623-24 stating that he was born at
Fordham  and the  son  of  Thomas Jenner,    a farmer.          Among his
contemporary fellow  students at Christ's College was the illustrious
John Milton.             He came to New England with his father,    and as Mr.
Jenner,      Jr. ,      received a grant of 45 acres at Weymouth at the same
time that his father was granted 18 acres.              He was admitted a free-
man of the Massachusetts Bay Colony,   6 Sept. 1639.    He was chosen
minister there,   but removed to Saco,   Me.,  before 16Apr. 1641.    He
 - 340 - 
336                                               JONES
was settled  there at  £47 per  annum.             The people  there were gen-
erally  inclined to  the  Church of England,   and he wrote Gov.  John
Winthrop on 6 Apr. 1646,   that he was "on the wing of removal.  "     He
soon returned to England,  and on 17 Apr. 1651,  was settled at Coltis-
hall,    county of Norfolk.          On the last-named date he sold his  library
in New England for  £50 to Gov. Edward Winslow,   who was then in
London.             He resigned as rector of the parish of Coltishall  in  1657.
Thomas Jenner of Charlestown granted unto  Elder Edward Bates
and John  Whitman of  Weymouth a dwelling  house at  Weymouth
(now in possession of John King),   two orchards and 21 acres,    12 acres
at  the   "westerne neck"  one-half acre upon Grape Island,  and 40
acres  "which is  my my own proper lott, " and 18 acres  "which was
my father's,  "   with the consent  of Mrs. Jenner,   28 Dec.  1649.    His
wife's  name was Ellen  -
He died in Ireland between 4 June,   1672 and 26 May,  1676.     (See
New York Genealogical and Biographical Record,  47:   114.)

1.   SIMON  JOY (Joseph,      Joseph,       Thomas¹)   was  son  of  Joseph
and Elizabeth (Andrews)  Joy,  born at Hingham,    28 Dec. 1697;    died
at Weymouth,   13 Apr. 1789.    He married at Hingham,   9 Feb.  1720-
21,       Hannah  Humphrey,     daughter  of  George  and  Elizabeth  ( —)
Humphrey of Hingham.     She was born at Hingham,   1 Dec.  1698 ;
died  in  1778.     He removed from  Hingham to  the  South  Parish  of
Weymouth about 1737,    and settled  near  Independence Square.            In
1751  he  was  styled  a trader,    originally  having  been  a weaver by
trade.
Simon  Joy  of  Weymouth,    yeoman,   " being  apprehensive  of  my
approaching change, "  made his  will,   10 Mar.  1789,    as follows :           "As
to my son William,    my deceased son Jonathan,   my son Nehemiah,
my son Isaac and my son Jacob,  I consider that they each have had
about their  parts already from my estate.                                   Unto my son David
my house,    barn and all  my buildings and my lands on both sides  of
the way near  my house,   and my lands in Weymouth and Braintree,
and appoint him executor. "     Witnesses:     James Torrey,    Asa White,
and David Joy,     Jr.
David Joy of  Weymouth,   gentleman,  gave bond as  executor with
James Torrey,   physician,   and Asa White,   cordwainer,   both of Wey-
mouth,      sureties,    5 May,    1789.    (Suffolk  Probate  Records,      88:    196,
198.)
Children,   born at Hingham:

7.   LIEUT.     DAVID  JOY ( Simon )  was born  near  1738;       died  at
Weymouth,     12 Sept.  1820,    aged 81  or 82 years.     He married (1)  at
Weymouth,    12 Jan.  1769,    Mrs.  Margaret (Torrey)  White,    widow of
Abner White and daughter of David and Elizabeth (Turner)  Torrey,
born at Weymouth,  25 Aug. 1741;  she died at Weymouth,    15 Sept.
1803,     in  her 63d year.        He married (2)  at Weymouth,  5 July,   1810,
Widow Lydia  Blanchard,     widow  of  Nathaniel  Blanchard  of  Wey-
mouth.           She was daughter of Samuel and Dorothy (Thayer) Blanch-
ard of Weymouth,  and died,  the widow of Lieut.   David Joy,   at Wey-
mouth,    11 May,   1848,   aged 82 or 83 years 7 months 9 days.         Her birth
was apparently not recorded on Weymouth town records.          Lieutenant
Joy inherited the Joy homestead near Independence Square,     South
Weymouth.         He served in the Revolutionary Army from 1776 to 29
Nov.  1777,      and rose to the rank of First  Lieutenant.
David Joy,    gentleman,    made his will  9 Mar. 1819,   mentioning wife

KING
1.   JOHN KING,   born near 1600,   undoubtedly came with Deputy
Governor John  Humphrey.       (Winthrop's History  of New England,
1:   160.)     On 2 Sept.  1640,   John King and his  wife Mary appeared
in Boston before Thomas Lechford and employed him to compound
their  accounts.           In his  Note- Book Lechford  calls  them " heretofore
servants  to  the word John  Humfrey,    Esqr.  "    He further  notes that
"They were bound to serve foure yeares only ... to be freed when
they came toNew England, "  and that " since his departure "  into New
England  " John  King  hath  served  John  Humfrey twelve  weekes. "
Winthrop  tells   us  that  Mr.  Humfrey  brought  ordnance,     muskets,
powder and sixteen heifers which were given by Mr. Richard Andrews
to the ministers of the plantations.          John King in the service  of the
Deputy  Governor  undoubtedly  assisted  him  in  getting  these  into
New England.         Mr.  Humphrey came before 3 May,   1631,   and land
was granted  to  him at  Saugus,    6 Mar.  1632-33.              He brought  his
property and his family to New England in July,    1634.    In view of
these  facts  we are justified  in  the inference  that  his  servants  John
Legg and John King came with him before 3 May,   1631.    (Massa-
chusetts  Bay Colony Records,    1:86.)
"
On 23 June,    1657,  John King ofWeymouth deposed before Thomas
Danforth  in  Middlesex  County Court  in  the case  of Joshua  Tead
versus Richard Collicut.     He stated that he was "about 57 yeares'
of  age  and " that  he was  with  Mr.  Richard  Colicut  in  Kenebeak
River        " in  May,      1656.    (The  Genealogical  Advertiser,     1:   90-
95.)    This deposition gives his approximate age as born near 1600.
John Humphrey came from  Dorchester in  the county of Dorset,
which is  six miles north from Weymouth,    and it  is likely that John
and Mary King came from the same locality.        Neither the marriage
of John Humphrey nor that of John King is  on record in the parish
of Holy Trinity in Dorchester.
John King,     Sr. ,    was a resident  of  Weymouth from 1639  to  1669.
He early had lands granted to him,  although the bounds only remain.
He had one of the great lots granted 2 Feb. 1651-52,   and John King,
seaman,     and John King,  planter,   each had lots in the First Division
and in the Second Division granted them 14 Dec.  1663.    (Weymouth
Land Grants,      281,     282,      283.)    He witnessed  a deed  from  Robin
Hoode,       of  Negwasset,    an  Indian,   to John Richards,   22 Apr.  1649,
and made oath to the same 22 Aug. 1654.    (Suffolk Deeds,   2:   52. )
Hewith others appears before the General Court in Boston,   4 Dec.
1638,      to  give  evidence  about the murderer which "they took from
the island.  "    (Records of the Court of Assistants,   2:  77.)
Hemarried Mary     , who was his wife 2 Sept. 1640.   (Lechford's
Note-Book,        308.)      He  married   (2),      near   1647,       widow  Dorothy
(Barker)  Hunt,   successively  widow  of            Barker  and  of  Enoch
Hunt of Weymouth.        Dorothie  King,   wife  of John King of Wey-
mouth,     seaman,    made her will  14 June,   1652,    bequeathing  to  her

married with  my now husband John  King;           .. the care of her  I

Kingsley of  Dorchester. "    To her daughter Ruth Barker and to her
daughter Susannah Heath other things.      Her husband John King to

WILLIAM KING,  aged 40,   Dorothy       ,  his wife,  aged 34,   Mary,
his  daughter,     aged  12,     Katheryn,    aged  10,     Hannah,     aged  6,     and
William,    his son,    aged 8 years,     sailed from Weymouth in  Dorset  on
or  near 20  Mar.  1634-35,    in  Rev. Joseph  Hull's  Company,    and ar-
rived  at  Dorchester  7 June,     1635.    As there is  no reference  to  his
name in the Weymouth Land Grants or other Weymouth records it
is  apparent  that  he did not  settle  there.        He evidently  settled  in
Salem,    and there died shortly before 25 Feb.  1650-51.        The settle-
ment of his estate shows that he had a widow,   Dorothie Kinge;    an
eldest  son,     William;   a second son,   Samuel,    then  18 years  of age;     a
third son John,   aged 13,   a daughter,   Mary,   then wife of John Scud-
der;  a second  daughter,     Katherine,     then  wife  of John  Swaysy;   a
third  daughter,       Hannah;    a  fourth  daughter  Mehitable,     aged  15;
and a fifth daughter,   Deliverance,   aged 9.    (Records of the Quarterly
Courts of Essex County,    1:   206.)
It  has been conjectured that he came from Sherborne in Dorset.
The baptisms,   marriages and burials of all Kings in that parish from
1545 to  1695 were published in Notes and Queries for  Somerset and
Dorset,     3 :    144-146,   and they show that one William King married
there,     17  Feb.  1616-17,     Dorothy Hayne,  but no positive  proof has
been found showing that these were the identical persons who came in
Hull's  Company.       (Notes  and  Queries  for   Somerset  and Dorset,
8:  358;   11:87. )

KINGMAN
1.   HENRY  KINGMAN was born in England near 1593 or  1594;
died at Weymouth,   5 June,   1667.    Henry Kingman,   aged 40,   Joane,
his  wife,       aged 39,     Edward Kingman,    his  son,   aged  16,      Joane,     his
daughter,    aged  11,     Anne,   his  daughter,     aged  9,     Thomas,      his  son,
aged 7,     John,    his son,  aged 2 years,   and John Ford,  his servant aged
30 years,     sailed from Weymouth in Dorsetshire on or  near 20 Mar.
1634-35 in Rev. Joseph Hull's  Company,   and arrived at Dorchester,
7  June,     1635.    (Register,   25:    14.)    He was made a freeman of the
Massachusetts Bay Colony,    3  Mar.  1635-6.              (Ibid.      3:94.)     Seven
lots  were granted to him at Weymouth,   viz. ,   twelve acres  " in the
westerneck first  given to John Whitmarsh,"  three acres "first  given
to  William  Smith,"  another  three  "first  given  to  Edward Poole, "
four  "first  given to George Allen,"  three "in  the Easterneck, "  two
"neere burying Iland, "  first given to Angell Hollard,   and six acres in
the  westerneck,      first   given  to  Samuel  Butterworth.          (Weymouth
Land Grants,    268.)     He was "lycensed to keepe the saide fferry  at
Waymothe"  during the pleasure of the General Court,  3 Mar.  1635-
36,   and was to take twopence apiece for transportation of people,   12
Mar.  1637-38.            Massachusetts  Bay Colony Records,   1:  165,    225.)
Hewas licensed to keep a house of entertainment at Weymouth,    6
June,     1637.     (Ibid.      199.)     He was a deputy from Weymouth to the
General Court 2 May,    1638,   27  May,    1652,   and 26 May,   1657;      and
was one of  a committee to lay out a highway from  Weymouth to
Dorchester,     25 Dec.  1648.    William Richards,    for  £50,     sells  him his
dwelling house and 20 acres  in Weymouth,    12 May,   1648.    A brief
abstract  of his will is  as follows :
"Henry  Kingman of  Waymoth,    aged 74 yeares  or  thereabouts,
being weake of boddy,"  made his  will  24  May,     1667,     and  it  was
proved  31  July,     1667.    To  his  son  Edward Kingman he  gave his
dwelling and 25 acres,   and that meadow that was John Allin's,    and
one acre " nearest  to my house of that which was Mr. Jeners. "    To
his  son Thomas Kingman other lands and two acres "that was Mr.
Jeners, " also  25 acres " near and above Samuell White's house. "    To
his son John Kingman lands "near his house, " and a meadow "which

1753,     reads as follows:     " We hear from Weymouth that on Thursday
last  was married'   there,    at  the hour of  12,     Mr.  Ephraim  Thair  of
Braintree,     being 84 years old,   to Mrs. Mary Kingman of that place,
aged 78,    it being about fifteen months since he buried his former wife
(with whom he had lived sixty years in the married state) ,   at which
time he was father,     grandfather  and great-grandfather  of sixty-six
male and sixty-six  female  children,    since  when there  has been an
increase of twenty more.       After the ceremony was over,    he returned
to his house in Braintree,   attended with a great concourse of people. "
Mary Kingman of Weymouth,   widow of Thomas Kingman,    was ap-
pointed  administratrix  29  May,     1752.    (Suffolk  Probate,   46:   217. )
Apparently his  estate remained unsettled  over  ten years.         Thomas
Kingman of Weymouth,   husbandman,     was appointed administrator
of the same estate,  24 Jan.  1755  (Ibid.      49:  817),   and  Capt.       Jacob
Turner,     Mr. James Humphrey and Mr. Thomas White,   all  of Wey-
mouth,    took the inventory 13 Feb. 1755;  total,   £307 17s.   7d.            Benja-
min Bicknell  and  Thomas  Kingman  appear  as  administrators  de
bonis non.              (Ibid.     921.)

LANE
THOMAS  LANE,    a  servant  to  John  Burslyn,    having  become
"lame and impotent " at Dorchester,   the General Court " ordered the
inhabitants of Wessaguscus to send for him and to pay for  keepeing
him dureing his  aboade att  Dorchest',"  on 3 June,  1634.    (Massa-
chusetts  Bay Colony Records,    1:   121.)    He is not mentioned in the
land  grants  of  Weymouth nor elsewhere  so far  as  is  known.              He
probably died unmarried,   and having acquired a residence in Wessa-
gusset  some  time  prior  to  3  June,   1634,   was  a servant  who came
with John Bursley in the Gorges Company in  1623.

LANG -LANGLEY
LANG
365
RICHARD LANG of Weymouth,   " clapboard ryver, "  made a com-
plaint  against  John Upham and William Smith in behalf  of  them-
selves and the rest  of the freemen of  Weymouth,    between 5 and 23
Oct.  1640.    He stated that he had been an inhabitant of Weymouth
by the space of six  years  last  past  or thereabouts  (from  1634)   and
ought to have a share in the neck of land in Weymouth,  but Upham
and Smith and the rest  of the defendants without the general  con-
sent of the town made an agreement  that  the  new planters  (Hull's
Company) ,    with Richard Silvester  and Arthur Warren,   should have
the said neck of land allotted them,   and that Lang " had three  acres
of  land going  to the mill; "   that  the defendants  unjustly  gave  the
same to  Richard Knight and they have " detayned"  his share of the
meadow and have assigned  great  lots  to  themselves  and have  not
assigned  any to  the  rest  of the  planters;     and lastly  that  said  de-
fendants " keepe the Towne booke disorderly some leaves having bin
cutt forth and some blotts and other defects there are therein, "  and
Lang " prayeth that the defendents may be enjoyned to appeare at
the next Court to answere and bring the said Towne booke.  "    (Lech-
ford's  Note-Book,     1638-41,   p.    338.)
At a particular court held at Boston,   29 Oct.  1640:    "It  is  ordered
Mr.  Stoughton  should  heare  busines  betweene  Rich'd  Lange & the
towne  of  Waymouth & Mr.  Stoughton  hath  power to  call for  the
towne booke,    & make report to the court if the cause do require it "
(Records  of  the  Court  of Assistants,    2:99.)    No further  record  of
this man has been found.

LENTHALL
REV.       ROBERT  LENTHALL was invited  to  become minister  of
the  First  Parish  of Weymouth before  13 Mar.  1638.    " Though  of
good report  in  England,"  Mr.  Lenthall was not settled there.         He
removed to Newport,   R. I. ,   and was admitted a freeman of the Rhode
Island Colony,  6 Aug. 1640.    By vote he was "called to keep a public
school  for  the  learning  of youth"  at  Newport,    20 Aug.  1640.    He
returned  to  England in  1642.    It  seems  that  "a disputation"  was
held at Dorchester at Captain Stoughton's between Mr. Lenthall and
the rest of the Elders of the Bay about some tenets that Mr. Lenthall
held,    on 11  Dec. 1638.    He said,  "I was for witnessing to the Truth,
unjustly cast out of my place,   to wch I was called by the people,   with
whom we sweetly agreed. "    At a General Court of Election held at
Newport 16 and 17  Mar. 1642,    Mr. Lenthall is referred to as "being
gonefor England. "     He was in charge of the parish of Barnes,   county
of Surrey,    from 1649 to 1658.    His wife Cicerley was buried at Barnes,
15 July,    1650.    He made his will at Barnes,    10 May,    1658,    and it  was
proved  3  Sept.  1658.    In  his  will  he  styled  himself  "clerke"  and
gave to  the  poor  of Barnes  20s.            His wife and children     to see his
bodie interred in the church yard of Barnes near to  the corner wall of
thewestand north side";  to RichardGoldston 10s.;  to NanBlinde 5s. ,
to poor James Bennett 5s.            "To my owne Brother Adryan Lenthall,
a ring of golde to be sent him if then liveing."    To my sister Downes
20s.                To my sister Kitely 20s.           To my sister Male a golde ring.         To
my sister  Hawes a ring  if  then living.       To my sister  Laughton  if
liveing  a ring  of 10s.     to be sent over to  her.             To my sister  Pickering
a gold ring to be sent her.      To Andrew Kitely a new suit ofcloathes
and 40s.      to put him out to some trade.      To my loveing  wife Mar
 - 372 - 
368                                                LEWIS
garett Lenthall threescore and five pounds which is a part of £100 I
promised to leave her.         Also £20 being parte of what Thomas Signall
oweth me.             Of the  £100 there  is  £10 to  be excepted upon a debt
paid to  Mr.  Barrat for  my wife.        For my two daughters  Marrian
and Nan £20 each and  £10 to  my daughter Nan because of the in-
firmitie in her sight.       My wife and two daughters Marrian and Nan
to be joint  executrices.          Mr.  Thomas Eayres  of Kensington,     gent.  ,
and  Thomas  Signall  of  Barnes,      overseers.          Proved  by  Margaret,

LONG
JOHN  LONG,  husbandman,    of Weymouth,    aged about 24 years,
deposed before Thomas Lechford,  24 June,   1641.    (Lechford's Note-

town Genealogies,    625.)
LOOMAN  (LUMAN)
Mrs.  ANNE LOOMAN died at Weymouth,   13 Aug. 1659.  Thom-
as White,    aged about 60 years,   and John Thompson,    aged about 40
years,      saith  that they were with Mrs. Anne Looman of  Weymouth
about six weeks since,    and ye  same day that she dyed she was in per-
fect  memorie;    she  made her  will  and made Hannah Jackson,      her
grandchild,     her  executrix,    and gave two shillings  to  John Monticue
(Montague) ,     her grandchild yt dwells at  the Eastward,    and left  all
ye rest of her estate to Hannah Jackson,  and appointed us to be over-
seers,    21 Oct. 1659.    Deposed by Thomas White and John Thompson,
20  Oct.   1659.    Inventory  taken 24 Sept.  1659,    by  Thomas White
and John Rogers and sworn to  by Hannah Jackson,    20 Oct.  1659.
(Register,      9 :        142.)    Perhaps  her  grandchild  Hannah  Jackson  was
the Hannah Jackson,    daughter  of Edmund and  Martha  Jackson,
born in Boston,   1 Mar. 1636-37,    who married John Andrews.
LOUD
1.   FRANCIS  LOUD appeared  at  Weymouth as  early  as  1722.
He was published there  20 Oct.  1722,    to  Onner Prince of Hull.     She
was the daughter of  Isaac and Mary (Turner)  Prince of Hull.           She
was born at Hull,  26 Oct. 1701,   and died at Weymouth,   18 Jan.  1777,
in her 76th year.           Francis Loud died at Weymouth,   2 or 3 Jan.  1774,
in the 73d year of his age.         He is said to have been born 26 July,   1700.
Elliott  Loud of  Weymouth,      housewright,      was  appointed  admin-
istrator  of  the estate  of  Francis  Loud,    late  of Weymouth,     house-
wright,     18 Mar.  1774.     (Suffolk Probate,    73:   601.)    Josiah White of
Boston,       yeoman,   and James  Burrell  of  Weymouth,    vitualler,     were
sureties.
All of the descendants  of  Onner (Prince)  Loud are eligible to be-
come members of the Mayflower Society.

LOVELL
•  1.   ROBERT  LOVELL,     a husbandman,       aged  40,       Elizabeth  his
wife,     aged 35,     Zaccheus his son,   aged 15,   Anne his daughter,    aged 16,
John his son,    aged 8,   Ellen his daughter,  aged 1 year,   James his  son
aged  1  year and Joseph  Chickin,    his  servant,     aged  16 years,     sailed
from Weymouth,   in Dorset,    on or near 20 Mar. 1634-35,     and arrived
at Dorchester 7 June,   1635.    He was a member of Rev. Joseph Hull's
Company,    and with the company removed to Weymouth that year.
He was made a freeman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony,   2 Sept.
1635.    He died at Weymouth shortly before 25 June,  1672.    Robert
Lovell  of Weymouth,  "being sicke & weake,"  made his  will 3 Apr.
1651,      and it  was probated 25 June,    1672.    To his  wife he gave the
use of his dwelling house and land " all the time of her Widow hood "
and then to his  son John " after  my Wives Widowhood,"  and four
acres  that was Carpenters,   and three acres bought of Hart,    and half
the meadow bought of Smith,    and half the meadow bought of Hol-
brook,    and my lot by the  Mill,   eighteen  acres.          To son James  his
great lot of 36 acres and other half of lots given to son John.           To his
son-in-law Andrew Ford,   one heifer.          To Ford's eldest son one heifer
and to his youngest son one calf.       To John Lovell's son my yearling
bull.          Wife executrix.         Witnesses:    Tho:   Dyer,   Tho:  Bayley.          Thomas
Bayley made oath to it, 25 June,   1672.    (Suffolk  Probate,   7 :    217.)

20.  GENERAL  SOLOMON  LOVELL  (David,4  Capt.      Enoch³)
was born at Abington,  1 June,   1732;   died at Weymouth,     9 Sept.
1801.    He married (1) at Weymouth,   19 Jan. 1758,   Lydia Holbrook,
daughter of  John and Sarah  (Hunt)   Holbrook,    born at Weymouth,
3 Sept.  1734;    she died there 21 May,    1761.    He married (2)  at Wey-
mouth,      May,     1762,    Hannah Pittey  (Petty),  daughter of James and
Hannah ( Reed)  Pittey,    born  at  Weymouth,    8 Dec.  1730;   she died
there 8 July,    1795,    aged 66 years.
He commanded the  Penobscot  expedition  in the  Revolutionary
War,     1779;      served  as  colonel  at  Dorchester  Heights,      1776;    com-
manded a brigade in the  battle  of Rhode Island,     and represented
Weymouth in the General Court several years.       (For details  of his
life and his  Journal,    15 July,    1779,    to  14 Aug.  1779,   see publication
of the Weymouth Historical  Society,   No. 1,  by Gilbert Nash,    1881.)
He resided  on Neck Street  near its  junction  with Green Street,
North Weymouth,   in the Capt.    Enoch Lovell house.
General Lovell made his  will,   13 Jan.  1798,    and it was proved 10
Nov. 1801.   He mentions his eldest daughter Lydia Beals,   his daughter
Hannah Lovell to have the place Ebenezer Hunt lives  on,    daughter
Mary Wild,      son James Lovell residue  except  two silver  porringers
which were given by their grandmother Pittee to Hannah and Mary.
(Norfolk Probate,    11981.)

LUDDEN   (LUDDAM)
1.   JAMES  LUDDEN,   was born  near  1611;   died at  Weymouth,
7 Feb.  1692-93.         He has been called an"old planter. "    In describing
his return from Plymouth Colony to Wessaguscus on 31 Oct.  1632,
Gov. John Winthrop said:     "When they [the company]  came to the
great  [North]    river,    they  were carried over by one Luddam,     their
guide (as they had been when they came,  the stream being very strong,
and up to the crotch),  so  the  governour  called  the  passage  Lud-
dam's Ford.                              So they came,   that evening to Wessaguscus where
they were bountifully entertained,   as before,  with store of Turkeys,
geese,    ducks,     etc.,   and the next day [Nov. 1]  came to Boston. "   (Sav-
age's  edition  of Winthrop's History  of New England,    1 :    110-111. )
James Ludden is the only known man of the name in New England
who could have rendered this service as guide.
At the General Court held at Newe Town,    1 Mar. 1635-36,       the
magistrates  refer  to  a suite  betwixte  David Johnson and William
Almy "concerning one James  Ludam sometimes [formerly]   servt  to
either of them"  in which a judgment of £5 was granted William Almy,
but upon consideration  the execution was respited and the parties
agreed  that  the widow of David Johnson shall pay five  nobles  to
Almy,     and James Ludam a similar  sum.           (Records of the Court of
Assistants,    2:      61.)    David Johnson probably came in the Mary and
John,    arriving at Dorchester near 30 May,   1630,    and William Almy
was at  Lynn before  14 June,     1631,     and the  probabilities  are  that
James Ludden was living at Wessagussett at the time that the passen-
gers of the Mary and John landed at  Nantasket.          They journeyed
overland  through Wessagussett from  Nantasket to  Dorchester,     ar-
riving at their destination near 17 June,  1630.
Hehad three lots granted to him early,  a great lot granted 2 Feb.
1651-52,     and eight acres in the First Division and twenty-four acres
in the Second  Division  granted,   14 Dec.  1663.    (Weymouth Land
Grants,    271,    281,   282,   283.)
He was to have 10  shillings  from  Cutshamache,    who warned him
to appear  in General Court and then did not come to  prosecute,   5
Mar.  1638-39.              ( Massachusetts Bay Colony Records,  1:  249),    and
the General Court remitted his fine for want of gunpowder,    2 June,
1641.     ( Ibid.     331.)

He deposed,   calling himself 74 years of age,  7 July,   1685.    "Through
the great disease and decay of old age" he made his will 2 Oct.  1688,

that place in the Woods called  Carpenter's  Plains;"  to his  son Jo-

acres in his house lot and two acres upon the island.         His son James
to have all remaining,   including  his homestead.       "If my son Joseph
should never returne nor be heard of any more," the lands given him
shall be confirmed unto his son James.         The use of his whole estate
to be at the dispose of his wife (not named) during her life,    provided
she do not dispose of it  from his children.        She to be executrix and
sons James and Banjamin executors.        His wife to have his  personal
estate  and to  bestow  what she  sees  meet upon his  grandchildren.

WILLIAM  MANLEY was  an inhabitant  of Weymouth,     1676 to
1687.    His first  wife  was Rebecca   -  He was not identical with
William  Manley  of  Boston,      1686  to  1689,     as  Savage  conjectured.
He married (2),   before 1687,     Sarah      , the mother of his last  child
on record.           He was a soldier in Capt.    Daniel Henchman's Company
in  1675,      in King Philip's  War,    and again in  Capt.    William Turner's
Company in  1676.    His heir was a claimant of Narraganset,      No.  5
(Bedford,       N.  H.) ,     in  1733.    (Bodge's Soldiers in King Philip's  War,
51: 240,    432.)     He died at Easton,   2 Dec.  1717.

MARTIN
ROBERT  MARTYN of Batcombe,   county of Somerset,    husband-
man,    aged 44 years,   and Joane Martyn,   aged 44,   his wife,    sailed  in
Hull's Company from Weymouth in Dorset on or near 20 Mar. 1634-
35.    He had ten acres  in the  East field  and twelve in  the  "wester
 - 419 - 
MAVERICK                                415
neck"   granted  to  him  with  three  other  lots.         (Weymouth  Land
Grants,     279.)     He was one of the first  purchasers of Rehoboth in
1643,       his  allotments  being  valued  at  £228  10s.          (Rehoboth  Vital
Records,    910.)    Hedrewlot 51 there,  30 June,  1644,  and was a mem-
ber of the first board of selectmen of Rehoboth chosen 9 Dec. 1644.
With Abraham Martin and Isaac Martin he became one of the earliest
settlers  of Rehoboth.           He was made a freeman of the Massachusetts
Bay  Colony,       13  May,      1640.    He was appointed  to  view  the  land
beyond Monotoquid Ryver and bring a plot to  the General  Court,
6 Sept.  1636.     (Massachusetts  Bay Colony Records,   1:  177.)    He
with others was appointed to measure three miles " southward from
the southermost part of the  Bay and run the east  line  to  sea, "  20
Nov. 1637,    and again to establish the bounds between "Mount Wool-
laston & Waymoth,"  22 May,     1639.     (Ibid.        211,    257.)
He made his  will 6 May,   1660,     referring  to his wife Joan and his
children,     to his brother Richard Martin and his children in Old Eng-
land,    to his elder brother Abraham Martin,  to his cousin Roger Clapp
of Dorchester.           His  widow Joannah  Martin  made her  will,   which
was probated 6 Apr.  1668,   in which she names her sister  Smith,    her
cousin  Clapp  and her kinswoman Jane  Clapp,     her  kinsman  John
Ormsby and her cousins Grace,     Thomas and Jacob Ormsby,   and her
brother  Upham's children at Malden.         (Register,  6:93;   7:   178.)
Joane was the daughter of Richard and Maria Upham of Bicton
in Devonshire.         (See Upham.)
.   ROBERT MARTIN,   son  of  Christopher Martin,   was baptized at
Batcombe,       25  Apr.  1597.    (Wells  Transcripts  of  Dwelly's  Parish

MAVERICK
SAMUEL  MAVERICK,    son  of Rev.  John  Maverick,       rector  of
Beaworthy,     county of Devon,   and minister  of the First Church of
Dorchester,       was born  in  England near 1602.    He called himself 63
years of age or thereabouts,  7 Dec.  1665.    (Suffolk County Deeds,   4:
328.)    He was one of the Gorges Company,   arriving at Wessagusset
about the middle of September,   1623.    He married,   near  1628,     Am-
yas  (Cole)    Thompson,      widow  of  David  Thompson,    a  Scotchman,
who came in 1623 and settled on a plantation at Little Harbor near
Portsmouth,       N. H.,   but removed,   near 1626,  to an island in Boston
Harbor,     where  he soon  died,     since  known as  Thompson's  Island.
David Thompson married in the parish of St. Andrew's in Plymouth,
Eng.  ,    18 July,  1613,   Amyas Cole,  daughter of William Cole of Plym-
outh.            Perhaps  her  mother was  Agnes  Bryant.         Amias  Maverick
wrote from  "Nottells  Iland  in  Massachusetts Bay, "  20 Nov.  1635,
to  Robert Trelawny of Plymouth,    Eng.,  requesting him to  see her
 - 420 - 
416                                 MEIGS -MERRITT
father,      and reminding Trelawny that he "loved  my first  husband"
and desired him to assist  her and "my fatherless  children.  "     (Tre-
lawny  Papers,       76-78.  )
Samuel Maverick was,    according to Josselyn,   10 July,  1638,       "the
only hospitable man in all the Countrey,  giving entertainment to all
Comers  gratis.  "     (Josselyn's   Two Voyages,    13.)    Maverick wrote,
30 May,    1669,    a letter in which he said:      "It is 45 yeares since I came
into  New England.                                I have been  heare  from  the  very  first
settling of N:       England,  by the English. "     ( Massachusetts Historical
Society  Collections,    Fourth  Series,     7 :    318,    and New England His-
torical and Genealogical Register,   39:    33-48;   69:    157.)     Mrs. Amias
Maverick was living 3 Sept.  1672.
MEIGS
VINCENT¹  MEIGS,  who died at  Hammonassett (East Guilford) ,
Conn. ,  hadadminstration on his estate granted to his son John Meigs
at a probate court held at Guilford,   Wednesday,  2 Dec. 1658.   (Meigs
Genealogy   169.)      No  positive  evidence  has  been  found  showing
whether  the father  ever  resided  in  Weymouth,    but his  son below
named first  appears in New England at Weymouth.
JOHN  MEIGS (Vincent)  was born in England on Wednesday,
29  Feb.  1612,    according  to  the Meigs Genealogy,    166.    The same
authority  further states that he was born in the parish of Bradford-
Peverell,      in Dorset,    which is  about eleven miles north of Weymouth
in  Dorset.                The parish  registers  of  Bradford-Peverell do not  exist
before  1653,      and the various  contributors  to  the Meigs Genealogy
fail to give any documentary evidence as to the origin of John Meigs
or how the fact of his birth is established.
However,     the  will  of  William  Frye of Weymouth,     made 9  Nov.
1643,    states that the testator's sister was the wife of John Meigs whose
name was  Thomasine  (Frye)  Meigs,   and that Walter Harris's  wife
Mary  (Frye)    Harris  of  Weymouth  was  another  sister,       and  that
Thomas Rawlin's wife Hannah (Frye)  Rawlins,    also  of  Weymouth,
was a third sister.
Child,   born at Weymouth:
John,       b.    29 Feb.  1640–41.

MORRELL
REV.    WILLIAM  MORRELL,  an Episcopal clergyman,   came with
the Gorges Company to Wessagusset Sept.  1623.   A William Morell,
probably  the  above  named,    matriculated  as  a sizar  at  Magdalene
College,     University  of  Cambridge,    in  1611,    and graduated A.B.  in
1614-15.                 (Catalogue of University  of Cambridge.)    In his  History
of  Plymouth Plantation,    Governor William Bradford said:
"About  ye  midle  of  September  [1623]     arrived  Captaine  Robart
Gorges  in  ye  Bay of ye  Massachusets,    with  sundrie  passengers  and
families,    intending  their  to begine  a plantation;     and pitched upon
the place Mr.  Weston's people had forsaken.         He had a commission
from the  Counsell of New-England,   to be generall Gove[rno]r of the
cuntrie,    and they appoynted for his counsell and assistance,   Captaine
Francis  West,    the  aforesaid  admirall,     Christopher  Levite,     Esquire,
and the Governo] r  of  Plimouth for the time beeing,    etc.
"The  Governo]r  brought  over  a  minister  with  him,       one  Mr.
Morell,         who,        about  a year  after   the  Governo]r  returned,       tooke
shipping from hence.      He had I  know not what power and Authority
of  superintendacie  over  other  churches  granted  him,   and  sundrie
instructions  for  that end;    but he never  shewed it,    or made any use
of it;     (it  should seeme he saw it  was in vaine;)   he only speake of it
to some hear [at Plymouth]  at his going away.         This  was in effect  the
end of  a 2 [second]     plantation  in  that  place. "     (Bradford's History
of Plymouth  Plantation,    1620-47,    published by The Massachusetts
Historical Society,    1912,    V.  1,      327,      337.)
While living  at Wessagusset  (Wessaguscusset),    Mr.  Morrell wrote
Nova Anglia,       a poem  in  Latin  hexameters,    and  translated  it  into
English   heroic  verse.            His  literary   productions  were  printed   in
London in 1625,   under the title:      " NEW ENGLAND.    |    OR |  A BRIEFE
|  ENARRATION |     OF    THE   AYRE,   |     EARTH,          WATER,         FISH   AND |
FOWLES  OF   THAT  COUNTRY.    |            WITH |     A  DESCRIPTION |         OF   THE
NATURES,    ORDERS,    HABITS,  ❘   AND RELIGION  OF  THE  NATIVES;   |         IN
|  LATINE  AND  ENGLISH   VERSE.    |            SAT  BREVÈ,      SI  SAT  BENÈ.  |
LONDON,     |                     IMPRINTED BY I.   D.  |          1625. "
This man who stood by the cradle of New England Puritanism is
not mentioned in Perry's History of the American Episcopal  Church
1587-1883.               All that  appears to  be known is  that while residing  at
Wessagusset  he  produced  the  earliest  American  poem  which  was
published.
